The payee or holder in due course files a written complaint before a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class with jurisdiction (ordinarily where the payee's bank branch lies), within one month of the cause of action; delay may be condoned for sufficient cause.
The Magistrate takes cognizance of the offence on the complaint; the complainant's evidence may be given on affidavit.
The offence is tried only by a court not below a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.

stages.stage: 5 · Issue of process (summons) to the accused
steps: The Magistrate issues summons to the accused. A summons may be served by speed post or an approved courier and is deemed served even if the accused refuses it.
The accused appears; the substance of the accusation is stated and the plea recorded. A s.138 case is tried as a summary trial.
The court may direct the drawer to pay interim compensation of up to 20% of the cheque amount.

The complainant's evidence is led, usually on affidavit, and the accused may cross-examine. The bank's dishonour slip is prima facie proof of dishonour, and the court presumes the cheque was issued for a debt or liability unless the accused rebuts it.

stages.prescribed: Endeavour to conclude within 6 months of filing
steps: After final arguments the Magistrate delivers judgment. The trial is conducted summarily and the court is to endeavour to conclude it within six months of the filing of the complaint.
On conviction the drawer is liable to imprisonment up to two years, or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both, and the court ordinarily awards compensation to the payee.
The offence is compoundable at any stage, so the parties may settle and close the case.
An appeal against conviction lies to the Court of Session. Where compensation or a fine was awarded, the appellate court may require the appellant to deposit a minimum of 20% of it.

institutions.summary: The police and the courts a s.138 case runs through, from central law - the Police Act, 1861 and the Constitution read with the BNSS. Each state's own Police Act and court rules fix the local ranks, units and establishment; those are layered on as each state is processed.

police.summary: The police hierarchy. The Police Act, 1861 constitutes the force under an Inspector-General with a Superintendent in each district; the modern rank ladder (Constable up to Director General) and the units are fixed by each State's Police Act. Senior ranks are Indian Police Service (IPS) officers recruited through the UPSC Civil Services Examination; the rest are the State Police Service.

ranks.name: Director General of Police & State Police Chief
ranks.who: The administration, supervision, direction and control of the entire State police, subject to the Government.
ranks.entry: An IPS officer of the State cadre already promoted to Director General, selected by the State Government under the State's Police Act.

ranks.name: Director General of Police
ranks.who: Apex rank; heads statewide wings and branches (crime, intelligence, armed police, etc.).
ranks.entry: IPS, via the UPSC Civil Services Examination, promoted over a career.

ranks.name: Additional Director General of Police
ranks.who: Heads a zone or a major functional wing.
ranks.entry: IPS, by promotion.

ranks.name: Inspector General of Police
ranks.who: Heads a zone or range or wing. The 1861 Act's Inspector-General was the historical head of the force.
ranks.entry: IPS, by promotion.

ranks.name: Deputy Inspector General of Police
ranks.who: Heads a police range - a group of districts.
ranks.entry: IPS, by promotion.

ranks.name: Superintendent of Police
ranks.who: District Police Chief - commands the whole police of a district. Registers and supervises serious cases.
ranks.entry: IPS (direct recruit, after serving as Assistant SP), or a promoted State Police Service officer.

ranks.name: Deputy Superintendent of Police
ranks.who: Sub-divisional officer; supervises a group of circles and stations.
ranks.entry: The State Police Service, via the State Public Service Commission, or promotion from Inspector.

ranks.name: Inspector of Police
ranks.who: Heads a circle; Station House Officer of larger stations; supervises the Sub-Inspectors under him.
ranks.entry: Promotion, or direct recruitment through the State Public Service Commission.

ranks.name: Sub-Inspector of Police
ranks.who: Station House Officer of most police stations - registers the FIR, investigates, files the charge-sheet.
ranks.entry: Direct recruitment through the State Public Service Commission, or promotion.

ranks.name: Assistant Sub-Inspector of Police
ranks.who: Assists the SHO; may hold charge of an outpost.
ranks.entry: Promotion, or the State Public Service Commission.

ranks.name: Police Head Constable
ranks.who: Senior constable; supervises constables and beat duty.
ranks.entry: Promotion from Constable.

ranks.name: Police Constable
ranks.who: The basic rank - patrol, guard, beat and first response.
ranks.entry: Direct recruitment through the State's police recruitment process; the entrant must meet the statutory eligibility and take the prescribed oath.

units.name: State Police Force
units.head: State Police Chief / DGP
units.who: One unified State force, divided into wings, units and branches by the Government.

units.name: Zone
units.head: ADGP / IGP
units.who: A cluster of ranges.

units.name: Range
units.head: DIG
units.who: A group of districts.

units.name: District
units.head: Superintendent of Police
units.who: The basic territorial police command.

units.name: Commissionerate (metropolitan)
units.head: Commissioner of Police
units.who: Unitary metropolitan policing for the larger cities a State notifies.

units.name: Sub-division
units.head: Dy.SP
units.who: A group of circles within a district.

units.name: Circle
units.head: Circle Inspector
units.who: A group of police stations.

units.name: Police Station
units.head: Station House Officer
units.who: The primary unit; its jurisdiction is notified and it must be functional at all hours.

units.name: Outpost / Beat
units.head: ASI / Head Constable
units.who: The smallest sub-units of a station for local coverage.

oversight.name: State Security Commission
oversight.who: Lays down policy and insulates the force from illegitimate pressure.

oversight.name: Police Establishment Board
oversight.who: Decides postings, transfers and promotions of officers up to a rank.

oversight.name: Police Complaints Authority
oversight.who: Inquires into serious complaints of misconduct against the police.

judiciary.summary: The court hierarchy a s.138 case moves through: the trial court is the Judicial Magistrate of the First Class; appeal lies to the Court of Session; revision and quashing to the High Court; and, by special leave, to the Supreme Court. Alongside the judges sits the court's ministerial establishment.

tiers.name: Supreme Court of India
tiers.who: The highest court. A s.138 matter reaches it only by special leave (art.136); its law binds every court in India (art.141).

tiers.name: High Court of the State
tiers.who: The State's highest court. In a s.138 case it hears criminal revisions and petitions to quash the complaint (s.482 CrPC / s.528 BNSS) and superintends the subordinate courts.

tiers.name: Court of Session (District & Sessions Court)
tiers.who: Headed by the District & Sessions Judge. It hears the first appeal from a s.138 conviction.

tiers.name: Chief Judicial Magistrate
tiers.who: Heads the magistracy of a district and has administrative control over the Judicial Magistrates.

tiers.name: Judicial Magistrate of the First Class
tiers.who: The trial court for a s.138 case: it takes cognizance of the complaint, tries it summarily, and on conviction sentences the accused.

roles.name: District & Sessions Judge
roles.who: Heads the district judiciary; hears sessions trials and s.138 appeals.
roles.entry: The Higher Judicial Service - direct recruitment of advocates with 7+ years' practice (art.233), or promotion from the subordinate judiciary.

roles.name: Judicial Magistrate (First Class)
roles.who: Tries the s.138 complaint - takes cognizance, records evidence, delivers judgment and sentence.
roles.entry: The State Judicial Service - a competitive examination for the civil-judge/magistrate cadre conducted by the High Court with the State Public Service Commission (Constitution art.234).

roles.name: Sheristadar / Chief Ministerial Officer
roles.who: Head of the court's ministerial establishment; signs and issues the summons 'by order of the Court'.
roles.entry: The district judiciary's ministerial establishment, recruited under the High Court's supervision and by promotion.

roles.name: Bench Clerk
roles.who: Maintains the court's daily records, exhibits and order sheet during hearings.
roles.entry: Ministerial cadre of the district judiciary.

roles.name: Registry / Scrutiny officer
roles.who: The court office that receives and scrutinises the filed complaint for defects before it goes for cognizance.
roles.entry: Ministerial cadre.

roles.name: Registrar (High Court)
roles.who: Heads the High Court registry - scrutiny, listing, custody of records.
roles.entry: A senior District Judge or a promoted officer of the establishment.

roles.name: Process server / Summons bailiff
roles.basis: Court ministerial establishment
roles.who: Serves the summons and warrants the court issues.
roles.entry: Ministerial cadre of the district judiciary.

roles.name: Stenographer / Interpreter
roles.who: Records dictation and interprets a deposition into the language the State has notified as the court language.
roles.entry: Ministerial cadre of the district judiciary.

story.summary: How a §138 cheque-bounce case runs in Gujarat, from filing to disposal - built from the Gujarat instruments, with every step citing the provision that governs it. Click any citation to open the exact text. Two things set Gujarat apart: the complaint costs three rupees to file, and for bank and NBFC cheque cases in Ahmedabad City the case runs in a SARAS court, where the electronic record is the primary judicial record and the magistrate may be sitting anywhere in the State.

roles.who: The payee or the holder in due course of the dishonoured cheque. Only this person can set a §138 case going, by filing the written complaint in their own name. In the Ahmedabad City SARAS courts the complainant is typically a bank or an NBFC filing in bulk.

Where duly authorised and personally aware of the transaction, files the complaint and deposes for the complainant. The e-Filing SOP requires the original power-of-attorney to be preserved permanently, not merely for two years - so the paper behind a bulk bank filing does not disappear.

The drawer of the cheque. Where the drawer is a company, the company and every person who was in charge of and responsible to it. In a SARAS case the accused must be physically present at the SARAS court or a remote point when the plea is recorded and when judgment is pronounced.

Stands behind the accused's bond. The presiding officer tests the surety's solvency himself by summary enquiry; a revenue solvency certificate is insisted on only in cases of doubt or for large sums, and moveable property suffices for a bond up to Rs.2,000. The intending surety applies in model Form No. 33.
The bank on which the cheque is drawn. Its return memo is the document that starts the clock, and the NI Act makes the bank's slip with the official mark evidence of dishonour.

Usually the bank official who proves the return. Examination-in-chief for the complainant is ordinarily tendered by affidavit; cross-examination is ordinarily in physical presence, at a Formal Witness Deposition Centre or a notified remote point. The court pays the witness bhatta, and unclaimed bhatta is remitted by money order fifteen days after final disposal.

Appears for a party on a vakalatnama, which every pleader must file in every class of criminal case in Gujarat. On the digital side the advocate is also the registered e-Filer - registered on the portal with the Bar Council certificate or I-card, and signing filings with a digital signature or an Aadhaar e-sign.

Carries the file through the registry - filing, clearing objections, collecting copies and following the matter. A recognised court-precinct role rather than a statutory office; the Gujarat instruments name the e-Filer and the Registry, not the clerk.
roles.basis: Court-precinct and registry practice - not a statutory office in the Gujarat rules

roles.who: Tries the §138 complaint - takes cognizance, examines the complainant, records evidence and delivers judgment. In a SARAS court the same officer is the 'Presiding Officer' who verifies the registered matter on the portal, digitally signs the exhibits, the orders, the depositions and the rojnama, and may sit anywhere in the State.

Heads the magistracy under which the SARAS N.I. Court establishment sits. The SARAS Rules apply to that establishment 'under C.J.M. Courts of Ahmedabad City' and to such other courts or classes of proceeding as the High Court notifies.

The ministerial establishment responsible for scrutiny, processing and maintenance of records. Scrutiny of e-filed complaints for technical compliance is its exclusive domain: it takes up a new complaint on the next working day, registers it or records objections in writing, and assigns the registered case to a court.

roles.role: Clerk of the Court / Senior Clerk
roles.who: Signs and seals the summons of a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class, or where there is no Clerk of the Court, the Senior Clerk or a clerk specially assigned that work in writing. In the Sessions Court the Clerk of the Court also certifies the typed copies of the record sent up in appeal.

The head ministerial officer. Under the Criminal Manual the Sheristedar signs and seals the summons of a Metropolitan Magistrate's court, keeps the property register and deals with copy applications. The Manual predates the BNSS, which no longer provides for Metropolitan Magistrates; in the Chief Judicial Magistrate courts the Senior Clerk does the corresponding work.

Handles cash, deposits and case property. Prepares and signs the Property Register, verifies muddamal against the police Pavti or Yadi before entry, and is among the officers before whom an intending surety presents the suretyship application. Officers dealing with cash, stamps or muddamal give security in the manner prescribed for the Nazir.

Runs the file through the hearing day and records the rojnama in CIS at the end of it. In a SARAS court the Bench Clerk places each case's physically produced documents in a sealed, marked envelope and keeps them ready for the court; physical documents are held by the Superintendent or Board Clerk. The Magistrate, though, must settle his own Board and not leave it to the Bench Clerk.

Sits at each end of the live link. There is a coordinator at the court point and at the designated place from which a person is examined or heard, though one is needed at the remote point only where a witness or an accused is being examined. Nominated by the High Court or the Principal District and Sessions Judge, and counter-signs a document sent back from the remote point.
Takes the magistrate's dictation of the order sheets, online during or after the hearing in a SARAS court; the typed order sheet is digitally signed before it is uploaded to CIS.

Interprets evidence given in a language the court or the accused does not understand. Sessions Judges, District Magistrates and Chief Metropolitan Magistrates are authorised to pay a reasonable sum for the service. In a remote hearing the fee of the translator or interpreter is borne as the court directs.

Serves the court's summons on the accused and executes any warrant that follows. It is a statutory duty of every police officer to do so promptly for every order lawfully issued by competent authority. A §138 case is a complaint case, so this is essentially the only role the police have in it.

steps: A cheque-bounce case is a complaint case. Only the payee or the holder in due course can start it, and the Magistrate can take cognizance only on such a written complaint - never on a police report.
It must be filed within one month of the cause of action, which arises when the drawer fails to pay within fifteen days of the demand notice served after dishonour.

In Gujarat the complaint is e-filed. The e-Filing SOP for the District Judiciary defines an 'Action' to include criminal complaints, which is what brings a cheque case inside the regime at all, and an advocate or a litigant in person files from anywhere through the portal or through a designated counter.

The complaint, the vakalatnama, the list of documents and the affidavits are signed with a digital signature or an Aadhaar-based e-sign; where the filer has neither, the physically signed papers are scanned and uploaded.

The court fee is three rupees. Schedule II, Article 1(c) of the Gujarat Court-Fees Act charges a flat three rupees on a writing containing a complaint or charge of any offence presented to a criminal court, whatever the cheque is worth, and section 4 forbids the document being filed at all unless the fee is paid. It is paid electronically.
Every pleader appearing for a party in any criminal court in Gujarat must file a vakalatnama; the fee on it is two rupees in a magistrate's court.

The date of e-filing is the date the filing is electronically received in the Registry on a working day, IST. Anything filed online after 1600 hours, or on a holiday, counts as filed on the next court working day - and no exemption from limitation is allowed because the portal failed. In a cheque case with a one-month window that clause bites directly.

Where the case is a cheque complaint by a bank or an NBFC in the Chief Judicial Magistrate courts of Ahmedabad City, e-filing is not optional: the SARAS Rules apply to that establishment and to cases e-filed under section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, and all complaints, applications and affidavits are e-filed on the designated portal.

process.stage: 2 · Scrutiny by the Registry and numbering
steps: Scrutiny of an e-filed complaint for technical compliance is the exclusive domain of the Registry - the ministerial establishment responsible for scrutiny, processing and maintenance of records.

The Registry takes up a newly e-filed complaint on the next working day. If it is in order the matter is registered under the appropriate case type; if defects are noticed, objections are recorded in writing and communicated for rectification, and only when every objection is cleared is the case registered and assigned to a court.

Once registered, the matter goes first to the presiding officer's account on the designated portal for perusal, then to the designated court staff, who assign bookmarks, exhibits and marks strictly in conformity with rule 76 of the Criminal Manual, and then back to the presiding officer to be digitally signed. Only then is it part of the official judicial record.

process.stage: 3 · Cognizance and examination of the complainant
steps: The Magistrate takes cognizance on the complaint and examines the complainant, and any witnesses present, on oath.

The Criminal Manual tells the Gujarat magistrate how to do it: the examination should as far as possible be taken immediately, and it must be full enough to let him judge whether there are grounds for proceeding. No reasons need be recorded for postponing the issue of process, but reasons must be recorded for dismissing the complaint.
Where that first examination of the complainant is reduced to writing, the Court-Fees Act charges a further ten rupees, unless the court remits it.

A §138 complaint is tried as a summary trial unless the Magistrate decides otherwise. The Criminal Manual's own gloss is that no sentence above three months may be passed in a summary trial and that the summons-case procedure is followed.

No summons or warrant issues until the list of prosecution witnesses is filed, and on a complaint made in writing a copy of the complaint must accompany the summons - the complainant supplies the copies.

The summons of a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class is signed and sealed by the Clerk of the Court, or where there is none by the Senior Clerk or a clerk specially assigned that work in writing by the presiding officer.

The complainant pays the process fee for service and execution - 30 paise for a summons or notice, Rs.1.25 for a warrant of arrest, a proclamation or a warrant of attachment. The table must be exposed to view in a conspicuous part of every court, in English and the regional language.
Service is the police's job: it is the duty of every police officer promptly to serve every summons and to obey and execute every warrant or other order lawfully issued to him by competent authority.

Where a witness is to be examined by video conferencing, the process must state the date, time and venue of the designated place, direct the witness to attend in person with proof of identity, and, if the examination is about a particular document, carry a copy of that document.

Documents filed electronically may in addition be served from the designated e-mail IDs of Registry officials to the e-mail address of the advocate or party. That sits alongside, and does not displace, the statutory modes of serving the demand notice and the summons.

In a SARAS case the accused must be physically present at the SARAS court, or at a remote point, when the plea is recorded. The plea is signed physically and the signed sheet is scanned into the record with self-attested photo identity.

The copies of the complaint, documents and statements the accused is entitled to are ordinarily furnished electronically - by e-mail, by a recognised messaging service, or on a storage device at the accused's cost - or to a person nominated by the accused or the pleader appearing for him. Only where the accused cannot receive them electronically are printed copies supplied free of cost.

A party, an advocate or an accused may otherwise appear through video conferencing; in a criminal case any party or witness may move a request for it, and an advocate may appear from the advocate's remote point.

The accused who answers the summons is released on a bond. Two rupees of court fee is charged on a bail bond or a recognizance for appearance, and the sufficiency of the surety is primarily the presiding officer's own responsibility - a revenue solvency certificate only where there is doubt, moveable property enough for a bond up to Rs.2,000.

The complainant's evidence may be given on affidavit and read in any inquiry, trial or other proceeding under the NI Act. In a SARAS court the examination-in-chief of the complainant's witnesses is ordinarily tendered by affidavit through electronic filing.

The Criminal Manual prescribes how an affidavit used in a criminal court is headed and entitled, and requires the officer administering the oath to read and explain it, and certify that he has, where the deponent has not read it or is blind, illiterate or ignorant of the language.

Cross-examination is not remote by default. The examination-in-chief of the accused, the accused's witnesses and all cross-examination are ordinarily conducted in physical presence before the court, at a Formal Witness Deposition Centre notified by the High Court, or at a Government-notified remote point; recording evidence by audio-video means is permitted only in the court's discretion and strictly under the Video Conferencing Rules.

Where a person does appear remotely, the court first satisfies itself who is on the screen, and a document is put to them through the document visualizer at the court point or by transmitting an image; a document at the remote point comes back as a hard copy counter-signed by the witness and the coordinator.

The cheque, the return memo and the notice stay physical. Original documents produced in court are retained through the trial for evidentiary purposes even though the e-Filing SOP excludes cheques from permanent preservation, and may be returned to the complainant only on his undertaking to produce them again, against an endorsement of the case and exhibit number.
Case property produced in court is entered in the Property Register in Form No. 51 immediately on receipt, and verified against the Pavti or Yadi before entry.

The evidence is recorded in Gujarati. In summons cases and summary trials the Magistrate makes a memorandum of the substance of the evidence in the language of the court; a memorandum in English is not necessary. An interpreter is paid where a witness gives evidence in a language the court or the accused does not understand.
Once the cheque and the signature are proved or admitted, the presumption under §139 works for the holder, and it is for the accused to rebut it on the balance of probabilities.

process.stage: 7 · The record - Roznama, exhibits and order sheets
steps: The Roznama in Form No. 41 is the case's running history. It must be a faithful account with a correct list and description of the exhibits, kept from day to day as an original document, and initialled or signed by the Magistrate at the end of each day's proceedings. Ministerial acts such as receipt of bhatta or process fees stay out of it.

In a SARAS court the rojnama is recorded by the designated staff member in the Case Information System under the Case Proceedings block at the end of each hearing date, then placed for the presiding officer's digital signature - and only then does it form part of the official record.

Every document bears an exhibit number and a serial number as it comes before the court; an order or document filed below an existing exhibit is sub-numbered under it - an order below Exhibit 5 becomes Exhibit 5/1, not a new exhibit.

Orders, judgments and depositions are generated directly in PDF and digitally signed by the presiding officer on the portal; order sheets may be dictated to a stenographer online during or after the hearing and are digitally signed before being uploaded to CIS.

Physically signed originals, once scanned and uploaded, are preserved in sealed and marked covers in the custody of the court staff; the Bench Clerk or another designated staff member keeps each case's physical papers in a sealed envelope marked with the case particulars.
The offence carries imprisonment up to two years, or a fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both; the court may also order compensation to the complainant.

In a SARAS court the accused must be personally present when judgment is pronounced. Where a person is produced on a warrant, or is to be committed to prison on a conviction warrant, the issue, execution and compliance of that process follow the ordinary procedure established by law - the remote court does not change it.
Fine, penalty or compensation may be accepted through the e-payment facility once it is enabled for the court, and by cash or another permissible mode until then.
The case may also end by compounding at any stage - the offence is compoundable, and a settlement between the parties disposes of it.

Certified copies are governed by Chapter XXII of the Criminal Manual, but in a SARAS court they are generated from the digitally signed electronic record on the portal, and those digitally signed electronic copies are certified copies for all legal purposes. Supply by e-mail or on a device costs a minimum of Rs.50 for up to 25 MB and Rs.50 for each further 25 MB, plus the cost of the device.

The record is not despatched to the record room until the appeal or revision period expires and any appeal or revision is disposed of; the electronic record on the portal is retained and destroyed under the same rules 361 to 367 of the Criminal Manual so far as they can apply.
Appeal from a §138 conviction lies to the Court of Session. Where the appellant is the convicted drawer, the appellate court must order a deposit of at least 20% of the fine or compensation.

On a direction from the appellate or revisional court the record and proceedings are transmitted electronically from the designated portal; the original record and hard copies go up only if that court so directs.

Revision and quashing go to the High Court of Gujarat, where a Single Judge hears applications on the criminal side. The matter is presented in the office of the Registrar, gets a filing number at once and a registration number only if there is no office objection, must be accompanied by the certified copy of the judgment or order challenged, and must be examined by the office within six days of filing.

Office objections are put up on a special notice board and must be removed within fourteen days, failing which the matter goes before the Court for orders. Where the office re-examines the court fee, a receipt of a payment made through the e-payment system may be required in place of a stamp.

vocabulary.gloss: The StateWide Access to Remote Adjudication System - Gujarat's cheque-case courts. Rule 1 applies the SARAS Rules to the SARAS N.I. Court establishment under the Chief Judicial Magistrate courts of Ahmedabad City and to cases e-filed under section 25 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Created by a Full Court resolution of 2 December 2024 and inaugurated on 7 December 2024, these are courts written for cheque cases alone: the complaint is e-filed, the magistrate may sit anywhere in the State and hear the case by video conferencing, and the electronic record on the portal is the judicial record.
vocabulary.source: SARAS Courts Rules, 2026, Rule 1
aka: StateWide Access to Remote Adjudication System

vocabulary.gloss: The principle that makes a SARAS court work: even though the presiding judicial officer is stationed somewhere else in Gujarat, adjudication through audio-video electronic means is a valid mode of adjudication. Rule 9 says so expressly, resting on the Government and High Court notifications that set the courts up. The place the officer sits is the remote adjudication point; scanned physical papers are verified there before being sent on to the SARAS court.
vocabulary.source: SARAS Courts Rules, 2026, Rule 9

vocabulary.gloss: The eGujCourtIS system, or any other portal the High Court notifies, on which a SARAS case is viewed, processed and stored. Complaints are e-filed at filing.ecourts.gov.in, but it is the designated portal that holds the judicial record - the complaint, affidavits, exhibits, orders, judgments and rojnama entries the court actually acts on. Defined in Rule 2(1)(e).
vocabulary.source: SARAS Courts Rules, 2026, Rule 2

vocabulary.gloss: The electronic record maintained on the designated portal - and, in a SARAS court, the primary and authoritative judicial record, not a copy of a paper file. Rule 3 puts everything in electronic form: complaints, affidavits, applications, evidence, orders, judgments and rojnama entries are accessed and acted on electronically, authenticated by a token-based digital signature or by a scanned physical signature with photo identity. This is the sharpest difference between a SARAS cheque case and an ordinary one.
vocabulary.source: SARAS Courts Rules, 2026, Rule 3

vocabulary.gloss: A place from which a person appears before the court through a live link. It includes a designated place notified for the purpose but not an advocate's own chamber, which the Video Conferencing Rules call the advocate's remote point. In a SARAS cheque case the accused may be at a remote point when the plea is recorded, and a witness may be examined from one. Defined in Rule 2(1)(l).
vocabulary.source: Electronic Communication Rules, 2025, Rule 2

vocabulary.gloss: The courtroom itself, or wherever the court is physically convened - the other end of the live link from the remote point. A coordinator sits at the court point as well as at the remote point, and a document at the court point is shown to a remote witness from there. Defined in Rule 2(1)(f).
vocabulary.source: Electronic Communication Rules, 2025, Rule 2

vocabulary.gloss: The person who runs the video link at each end. Rule 9 requires a coordinator both at the court point and at the designated place from which a person is to be examined or heard, though one is needed at the remote point only where a witness or an accused is being examined. The High Court or the Principal District and Sessions Judge nominates them, and the Act of showing a document to a remote witness ends with the hard copy being counter-signed by the witness and the coordinator.
vocabulary.source: Electronic Communication Rules, 2025, Rule 9

vocabulary.gloss: The audio-video connection by which a witness, an accused, a party or an advocate is required to be virtually present in the courtroom. Defined in Rule 2(1)(k) of the Video Conferencing Rules; it is the mechanism a SARAS hearing runs on.
vocabulary.source: Electronic Communication Rules, 2025, Rule 2

vocabulary.gloss: Video conferencing and the other electronic modes recognised by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita. Rule 5 lets them be used at all stages of a judicial proceeding where a person required to be present is not physically in the courtroom, and makes clear that such a proceeding is a judicial proceeding to which the BNSS, the Contempt of Courts Act, the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam and the IT Act all apply.
vocabulary.source: Electronic Communication Rules, 2025, Rule 5

vocabulary.gloss: A centre notified by the High Court of Gujarat where a witness deposes, as an alternative to attending the SARAS court in person. Rule 6.2 says the examination-in-chief of the accused and the cross-examination of witnesses are ordinarily conducted in physical presence before the court, at an FWDC, or at a Government-notified remote point - so in a cheque case the affidavit goes in electronically but the cross-examination usually happens face to face somewhere.
vocabulary.source: SARAS Courts Rules, 2026, Rule 6

vocabulary.gloss: The camera at the court point that transmits a document to a person at a remote point. Rule 14 is how the three documents a cheque case is fought over - the cheque, the return memo and the demand notice - are actually put to a witness or an accused who is not in the courtroom: by document visualizer, or, failing that, by sending an image through the designated software or official e-mail. Where the document is at the remote point, the hard copy counter-signed by the witness and the coordinator must also be despatched to the court point.
vocabulary.source: Electronic Communication Rules, 2025, Rule 14

vocabulary.gloss: The hardware-token Digital Signature Certificate by which a document is authenticated in a SARAS court. Rule 3.4 allows only two modes of authentication: a token-based DSC, or a physical signature scanned and uploaded with self-attested photo identity where the person has no token. The presiding officer signs orders, judgments, depositions and the rojnama with the token, and it is that signature that makes the electronic document part of the official record.
vocabulary.source: SARAS Courts Rules, 2026, Rule 3

vocabulary.gloss: The registered user who files electronically - an advocate, or a litigant in person, registered on the e-filing portal under the Gujarat e-Filing SOP. An advocate registers with the Bar Council certificate or I-card, a litigant in person with a Government photo identity, and a login ID issues on the next working day. Defined in clause 2.8.
vocabulary.source: e-Filing SOP for the District Judiciary, 2024, Clause 2

vocabulary.gloss: The staffed counter where a person who cannot use the e-filing portal can still file electronically - at an eSewa Kendra, a Central Filing Centre or a helpdesk in the court complex. Clause 2.5 defines them and clause 3.3 gives the right to use them on payment of the stipulated charges; the SARAS Rules repeat the right in rule 4.3. Filing through a designated counter closes at 1600 hours on a court working day.
vocabulary.source: e-Filing SOP for the District Judiciary, 2024, Clause 2

vocabulary.gloss: The defect the office notes against a filing, and the clock that runs on it. On the High Court's criminal side rule 340 requires the office objections to be put up on a special notice board, with fourteen days for the advocate or applicant to remove them, failing which the matter goes before the Court for orders. The district-court counterpart is the Registry's written 'Objections' under the e-Filing SOP, notified by e-mail, SMS or web hosting.
vocabulary.source: Gujarat High Court Rules, 1993, Rule 340

vocabulary.gloss: The number a criminal matter gets on presentation, before it is registered. Rule 333 gives every criminal main matter a filing number first; a registration number issues only if there is no office objection. The same two-step appears in the e-filing SOP, where the filing or registration number is notified to the advocate or litigant once the e-filing is accepted. Until the matter is registered it is not a numbered case.
vocabulary.source: Gujarat High Court Rules, 1993, Rule 333

vocabulary.gloss: Three rupees. Schedule II, Article 1(c) of the Gujarat Court-Fees Act, 2004 charges a flat three rupees on a writing containing a complaint or charge of any offence presented to any criminal court, whatever the cheque is worth - not a fee scaled to the amount, as in Kerala. Section 4 makes it a gate rather than a formality: a chargeable document may not be filed, exhibited or recorded unless the fee has been paid. It is part of why banks and NBFCs file cheque cases in Gujarat in bulk.
vocabulary.source: Gujarat Court-Fees Act, 2004, Schedule II, Article 1

vocabulary.gloss: What the complainant pays for the court to serve its summons and execute its warrants. The Criminal Manual's table, made under the court-fees power and confirmed by the State Government, charges 30 paise for every summons or notice and Rs.1.25 for every warrant of arrest, proclamation or warrant of attachment in a case of an offence for which the police may not arrest without a warrant - which is what a §138 case is. No fresh fee is charged on a re-issue, and the court may remit the fee where a party cannot pay. Section 33 of the Court-Fees Act requires the table to be displayed in every court in English and the regional language.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 41

vocabulary.gloss: The money a court pays a witness for attending - travelling and subsistence expenses, deposited by the party who summoned them. Rule 208 says bhatta not claimed in person within fifteen days of final disposal is remitted by money order, and if that fails it goes on the Criminal Deposit Register or to Government. Rule 76 expressly keeps the receipt of bhatta out of the Roznama as a ministerial act. In a cheque case it is what it costs to bring the bank witness to court.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 208

vocabulary.gloss: The document by which a party authorises a pleader to appear and act. Rule 135 requires it from every pleader appearing for any party in every class of case in every criminal court in Gujarat, including appeals and revisional and miscellaneous applications, excepting only the Public Prosecutor, a court-appointed defence pleader, an amicus curiae, and a pleader briefed by another pleader already on record. Schedule II, Article 12 of the Court-Fees Act prices it at two rupees to a criminal court other than a District or Sessions Court or the High Court. On e-filing the signed original must be preserved for at least two years after final disposal.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 135

vocabulary.gloss: Gujarati is the language of the criminal courts of Gujarat. Rule 148 requires the magistrate, in summons cases and summary trials, to make the memorandum of the substance of the evidence in Gujarati, and in warrant cases to take the evidence down as a narrative in Gujarati; a memorandum in English is not necessary. The e-Filing SOP carries the rule into the digital layer - a document typed in the local language in a trial court must use LOHIT Gujarati Unicode and be OCR-enabled for Gujarati.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 148

vocabulary.gloss: The rule that decides what happens to the paper once the case is electronic. Clause 10 of the e-Filing SOP requires originals of scanned documents to be preserved for production or inspection as the Bench directs; the signed vakalatnama, the notarised affidavit and anything whose authenticity is likely to be questioned for at least two years after final disposal including appeal; and a negotiable instrument other than a cheque, a power-of-attorney, a trust, a will and a conveyance permanently. Cheques are the express exception - so the SARAS Rules step in and require the original cheque to be retained through the trial, and let it be returned to the complainant only against an undertaking and an endorsement of the case and exhibit number.
vocabulary.source: e-Filing SOP for the District Judiciary, 2024, Clause 10

vocabulary.gloss: The date the case counts as filed - which in a cheque case decides limitation. Clause 14 makes it the date the action is electronically received in the Registry within the prescribed time on a working day, on Indian Standard Time. An online filing after 1600 hours is treated as filed on the next court working day, as is anything filed on a holiday or a day the court is closed, and no exemption from limitation is allowed because the portal failed. Since a §138 complaint must be filed within one month of the cause of action, this clause bites directly.
vocabulary.source: e-Filing SOP for the District Judiciary, 2024, Clause 14

vocabulary.gloss: The running record of a criminal case in Gujarat - the proceeding sheet in Form No. 41, kept in Gujarati in the magistrates' courts. Rule 76 requires it to be a faithful history of the case and to carry a correct list and description of the exhibits, to be kept from day to day as an original document, and to be initialled or signed by the magistrate at the end of each day's proceedings. Ministerial acts such as the receipt of bhatta or process fees stay out of it. In a SARAS court the same record is entered by the designated staff member in the Case Information System under the Case Proceedings block and then digitally signed by the presiding officer.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 76

vocabulary.gloss: A document brought on the record and given a number. Rule 76 requires every document in the case to bear an exhibit number and a serial number as it comes before the court, and to be listed and described in the Roznama. The SARAS Rules keep the same scheme in the digital record: the designated staff member assigns bookmarks, exhibits and marks strictly in conformity with rule 76, and an order or document filed in continuation of an existing exhibit is sub-numbered below it - an order below Exhibit 5 becomes Exhibit 5/1, not a new exhibit.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 76

vocabulary.gloss: Case property produced in court. Rule 216 requires muddamal to be entered in the Property Register in Form No. 51 immediately on receipt, and rule 219 requires the article to be verified against the Pavti or Yadi the police produce in duplicate before it is entered. In a cheque case the muddamal that matters is the original cheque, the return memo and the demand notice, which the SARAS Rules say are retained for evidentiary purposes through the trial and may be returned to the complainant only on his undertaking to produce them when ordered.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 216

vocabulary.gloss: The head ministerial officer of a court. Rule 48(3) makes the officer performing the duties of Sheristedar the person who signs and seals a summons issued by a Metropolitan Magistrate's court; rule 383 puts copy applications in the same hands; rules 216 and 219 make the Sheristedar responsible for the property register. The Criminal Manual was written when Ahmedabad had Metropolitan Magistrates - the BNSS no longer provides for them, and the Ahmedabad City courts in which the SARAS establishment sits are Chief Judicial Magistrate courts, where the Senior Clerk performs the corresponding work.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 48

vocabulary.gloss: The officer who signs and seals the court's process. Rule 48(2) lets a summons issued by a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class be signed and sealed by the Clerk of the Court, and where there is none, by the Senior Clerk or the clerk specially assigned that work in writing by the presiding officer. In the Sessions Court the Clerk of the Court also certifies the typed copies of the record sent up to the High Court in appeal.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 48

vocabulary.gloss: The court officer who handles cash, deposits and case property. Rules 216 and 219 make the Nazir primarily responsible for preparing and signing the Property Register in the Sessions Court and for verifying muddamal against the police Pavti or Yadi before it is entered; rule 28 puts him among the officers before whom an intending surety presents the application for suretyship; rule 408 requires officers dealing with cash, stamps or muddamal to give security in the manner prescribed for the Nazir.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 216

vocabulary.gloss: The staff member attached to the court who runs the file through the day. In a SARAS court rule 3.12 makes the Bench Clerk, or another designated ministerial staff member, place the physically produced documents of each case in a sealed envelope marked with the case particulars and keep them ready for the court; rule 13.1 puts physical documents in the custody of the Superintendent or Board Clerk. Rule 89 of the Criminal Manual cuts the other way on listing - the magistrate must settle his own Board and not leave it to the Bench Clerk.
vocabulary.source: SARAS Courts Rules, 2026, Rule 3

vocabulary.gloss: The ministerial establishment of the court, responsible for scrutiny, processing and maintenance of records - defined in that form in Rule 2(1)(i) of the SARAS Rules. It is the Registry, and only the Registry, that scrutinises an e-filed complaint for technical compliance (rule 3.10): it takes up a newly e-filed complaint on the next working day, registers it under the appropriate case type if it is in order, and otherwise records objections in writing for rectification before the case is registered and assigned to a court.
vocabulary.source: SARAS Courts Rules, 2026, Rule 2

vocabulary.gloss: The person who stands behind the accused's bond and undertakes to secure their appearance. Rule 28 makes the sufficiency of the surety primarily the presiding officer's own responsibility, to be tested by such summary enquiry as he thinks fit; a revenue solvency certificate is to be insisted on only in cases of doubt or large sums, affidavits may be accepted in proof of solvency, and for a bond up to Rs.2,000 moveable property and assets are enough. The intending surety applies in model Form No. 33. In a cheque case the accused who answers summons is released on a bond, and Schedule II, Article 10 of the Court-Fees Act charges two rupees on it.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 28

vocabulary.gloss: Where the file goes when the case is over. Rule 361 says the record of a substantive criminal proceeding is not due for despatch to the record room until the appeal or revision period expires, and where an appeal or revision has been instituted, not until it is disposed of; records are kept intact in institution order for a further two months before filing orders are taken. The SARAS Rules carry the same regime to the digital side - the maintenance, classification, retention and destruction of electronic records on the designated portal are governed by rules 361 to 367 of the Criminal Manual so far as they can apply.
vocabulary.source: Criminal Manual, 1977, Rule 361

vocabulary.gloss: The hinge between the court and the police in a cheque case. Section 64(a) of the Gujarat Police Act makes it the duty of every police officer promptly to serve every summons and to obey and execute every warrant or other order lawfully issued to him by competent authority. A §138 case is a complaint case, so the police have no investigation to do - but the summons to the accused and any warrant that follows non-appearance are served and executed under this section.
vocabulary.source: Gujarat Police Act, 1951, Section 64

vocabulary.gloss: A Gujarat police recruit of the lowest grade. Section 2(4) defines 'constable' as a police officer of the lowest grade and expressly includes a Lok Rakshak, so a Lok Rakshak carries a constable's powers and duties under the Act - including the section 64 duty to serve the court's summons.
vocabulary.source: Gujarat Police Act, 1951, Section 2

vocabulary.gloss: The officer whose orders a police officer is bound to obey and execute under section 64. Section 2(3) defines it by area: in an area for which a Commissioner of Police has been appointed under section 7, the Commissioner; elsewhere the District Magistrate, the District Superintendent, or an Additional Superintendent specially empowered by the State Government. It is the term the service-of-process duty is written in.
vocabulary.source: Gujarat Police Act, 1951, Section 2

vocabulary.gloss: The head of policing for a city area. Section 7 lets the State Government appoint a Commissioner of Police, and an Additional Commissioner, for any notified area, and takes that area out of the charge of the District Magistrate and the District Superintendent. This matters concretely for a Gujarat cheque case because the SARAS establishment sits under the Chief Judicial Magistrate courts of Ahmedabad City, a commissionerate; section 12 lets the Commissioner constitute police divisions under a Superintendent and sections under an Inspector of Police.
vocabulary.source: Gujarat Police Act, 1951, Section 7

vocabulary.gloss: The district police command. Section 8 lets the State Government appoint a Superintendent, and one or more Additional, Assistant and Deputy Superintendents, for each district. Outside the commissionerate cities the District Superintendent heads the machinery that serves a magistrate's summons and executes his warrants, and is a competent authority for the purposes of section 64.
vocabulary.source: Gujarat Police Act, 1951, Section 8

vocabulary.word: Director General and Inspector General of Police
vocabulary.gloss: The head of the Gujarat police. Section 5A requires the State Government to appoint a Director General and Inspector General of Police for the overall direction and supervision of the force; section 6 provides for the Inspector General and for Additional and Deputy Inspectors General. Superintendence of the whole force vests in the State Government under section 4, and there is one police force for the whole of Gujarat under section 3.
vocabulary.source: Gujarat Police Act, 1951, Section 5
vocabulary.deep_link: #words?state=gujarat&term=director general and inspector general of police

vocabulary.gloss: Gujarat's police oversight body for serious complaints. Section 32G lets it look into complaints against police officers of the rank of Deputy Superintendent and above for serious misconduct, dereliction of duty or misuse of powers not covered by another commission; it may require information, enforce attendance and take evidence on oath like a civil court, and recommend action to the State Government. Section 32H establishes a District Police Complaints Authority for the ranks below.
vocabulary.source: Gujarat Police Act, 1951, Section 32G

institutions.summary: The two institutions a §138 case runs through on the ground in Gujarat - the police and the courts - with their hierarchy, the people in each role and where each comes from in law. Grounded in the Gujarat Police Act, 1951 for the police, and in the Constitution, the BNSS, the Criminal Manual, the Gujarat High Court Rules and the SARAS Rules for the courts.

police.summary: One Police Force for the whole of Gujarat (§3), with superintendence vested in the State Government (§4). The Act does not enumerate the ranks the way Kerala's does: §5(a) leaves the number, ranks, organisation, powers and duties of the force to the State Government by general or special order, and the Act names only the senior offices. A §138 case rarely touches the police at all - it is a complaint, not an FIR case - but §64(a) makes serving the court's summons and executing its warrants a police duty.

ranks.name: Director General and Inspector General of Police
ranks.who: Appointed by the State Government for the overall direction and supervision of the police force.
ranks.entry: An IPS officer of the State cadre, appointed by the State Government.

ranks.name: Inspector General of Police
ranks.who: Appointed for the direction and supervision of the force, with the powers, functions and authority the Act or Government orders provide.
ranks.entry: IPS, by promotion.

ranks.name: Additional and Deputy Inspector General of Police
ranks.who: May exercise any of the Inspector General's powers as the State Government directs, and aid and assist him.
ranks.entry: IPS, by promotion.

ranks.name: Commissioner of Police
ranks.who: Heads policing for a notified city area, which is taken out of the charge of the District Magistrate and the District Superintendent. The competent authority for that area - relevant here because the SARAS cheque courts sit under the C.J.M. courts of Ahmedabad City.
ranks.entry: A senior IPS officer, appointed by the State Government.

ranks.name: District Superintendent of Police
ranks.who: Commands the police of a district, subject to the orders of the Inspector General and the District Magistrate. A competent authority outside the commissionerates.
ranks.entry: IPS, or a promoted State Police Service officer.

ranks.name: Additional, Assistant and Deputy Superintendent of Police
ranks.who: Appointed for a district or part of one; an Additional Superintendent may be empowered to exercise all the District Superintendent's powers, and other powers may be delegated to an Assistant or Deputy Superintendent.
ranks.entry: IPS (Assistant Superintendent, as a direct recruit) or the Gujarat Police Service.

ranks.name: Inspector of Police
ranks.who: Each section of a police division is in charge of an Inspector of Police. Appointed by the Commissioner for his area and by the Inspector General elsewhere; every officer of the grade of Inspector or below receives a certificate of appointment.
ranks.entry: Gujarat Police Service, by direct recruitment or promotion.

ranks.name: Sub-Inspector and Assistant Sub-Inspector of Police
ranks.who: The station-level ranks. They are not enumerated in the Act - the ranks and organisation of the force are what the State Government determines under §5(a) - but they hold a certificate of appointment under §14 and the §64 duties.
ranks.entry: Gujarat Police Service, by direct recruitment or promotion.

ranks.name: Constable (including Lok Rakshak)
ranks.who: A police officer of the lowest grade, expressly including a Lok Rakshak. Serves the court's summons and assists in executing its warrants.
ranks.entry: Direct recruitment to the Gujarat Police.

ranks.name: Special Police Officer
ranks.who: A person appointed in writing by the Commissioner, District Superintendent or a specially empowered Magistrate to assist the force on an occasion of apprehended riot or grave disturbance, with the same powers and duties as an ordinary police officer while so serving.
ranks.entry: Appointed ad hoc by written order.

units.name: Gujarat Police (State)
units.head: Director General and Inspector General of Police
units.who: One force for the whole State, its numbers, ranks and organisation determined by the State Government.

units.name: Commissionerate (city area)
units.head: Commissioner of Police
units.who: A notified city area under a Commissioner, outside the charge of the District Magistrate and District Superintendent. Ahmedabad City, where the SARAS cheque courts sit, is one.

units.name: District
units.head: District Superintendent of Police
units.who: The territorial command outside the commissionerates; the District Magistrate controls the force in the district for the purposes of the Act.

units.name: Police division
units.head: Superintendent of Police
units.who: Constituted within a Commissioner's area, subject to the control of the State Government.

units.name: Section
units.head: Inspector of Police
units.who: A sub-division of a police division, in charge of an Inspector of Police.

units.name: Police station
units.head: Station House Officer
units.basis: The primary territorial unit. The Gujarat Police Act does not constitute police stations - their limits are fixed administratively and the officer in charge draws his powers from the BNSS.
units.who: Where the court's summons in a cheque case is sent for service.

oversight.name: State Security Commission
oversight.who: Advises the State Government on policy guidelines for the police, helps identify performance indicators, and periodically reviews the force's performance.

oversight.name: Police Establishment Board
oversight.who: Chaired ex officio by the Director General and Inspector General of Police; deals with postings, transfers and service matters of the force.

oversight.name: State Police Complaints Authority
oversight.who: Looks into complaints of serious misconduct, dereliction of duty or misuse of powers against officers of the rank of Deputy Superintendent and above; may enforce attendance and take evidence on oath, and recommends action. A District Police Complaints Authority covers the ranks below.

oversight.name: District Magistrate
oversight.who: Controls and supervises the police force in the district for the purposes of the Act and may require reports from the District Superintendent.

judiciary.summary: The court hierarchy a §138 case moves through in Gujarat: the trial court is the Judicial Magistrate of the First Class - and, for bank and NBFC cheque cases in Ahmedabad City, the SARAS N.I. Court under the Chief Judicial Magistrate there. Appeal lies to the Court of Session; revision and quashing to the High Court of Gujarat, where a Single Judge hears them. Alongside the judges sits the court's ministerial establishment, whose offices the Criminal Manual, 1977 still names in pre-BNSS language.

tiers.name: Supreme Court of India
tiers.who: The highest court. A §138 matter reaches it only by special leave; its law binds every court in India.

tiers.name: High Court of Gujarat
tiers.who: Hears criminal revisions and petitions to quash a cheque complaint, and superintends the courts below. A Single Judge takes the criminal list. It also makes the rules this whole layer runs on - the Criminal Manual, the e-Filing SOP, the Video Conferencing Rules and the SARAS Rules.
tiers.role: Revision, quashing, writ, superintendence and rule-making

tiers.name: Court of Session (District & Sessions Court)
tiers.who: Headed by the District & Sessions Judge; hears the first appeal from a §138 conviction, and orders the appellant's deposit of at least 20% of the fine or compensation.

tiers.name: Chief Judicial Magistrate
tiers.who: Heads the magistracy of a district. The SARAS N.I. Court establishment sits under the C.J.M. courts of Ahmedabad City.
tiers.role: Administrative head of the magistracy; host of the SARAS establishment

tiers.name: SARAS N.I. Court (remote adjudication)
tiers.who: Gujarat's dedicated cheque-case court: mandatory e-filing, hearings by audio-video means, the electronic record on the designated portal as the primary judicial record, and a presiding officer who may be stationed anywhere in the State. Adjudication in that mode is expressly a valid mode of adjudication.
tiers.role: The §138 trial court for bank and NBFC cases in Ahmedabad City

tiers.name: Judicial Magistrate of the First Class
tiers.who: The trial court for a §138 case everywhere else in Gujarat: takes cognizance of the complaint, examines the complainant, tries the case summarily and, on conviction, sentences the accused.

roles.name: District & Sessions Judge
roles.who: Heads the district judiciary and hears §138 appeals. The Principal District and Sessions Judge also nominates the video-conferencing coordinators for the courts in his jurisdiction.
roles.entry: The Higher Judicial Service - direct recruitment of advocates with seven years' practice, or promotion from the subordinate judiciary.

roles.name: Judicial Magistrate (First Class)
roles.who: Tries the §138 complaint - cognizance, examination of the complainant, evidence, judgment and sentence.
roles.entry: The Gujarat Judicial Service - the Civil Judge examination conducted by the High Court of Gujarat.

roles.name: Presiding Officer of a SARAS court
roles.who: The magistrate nominated to a SARAS N.I. Court. Verifies the registered matter on the portal, digitally signs the exhibits, orders, judgments, depositions and the rojnama, and may sit at a remote adjudication point anywhere in the State.
roles.entry: A judicial officer of the Gujarat Judicial Service nominated by the High Court to the SARAS establishment.

roles.name: Registrar (High Court)
roles.who: All criminal matters are presented in the office of the Registrar. The office gives a filing number, examines the matter within six days, notifies office objections on a special notice board and gives a registration number when they are cleared.
roles.entry: Judicial or ministerial service of the High Court of Gujarat.

roles.name: Registry (district judiciary)
roles.who: Scrutinises the e-filed complaint on the next working day, registers it or records written objections, and assigns the registered case to a court. Technical scrutiny is its exclusive domain.
roles.entry: Ministerial establishment of the district judiciary.

roles.name: Sheristedar / Senior Clerk
roles.who: The head ministerial officer of a magistrate's court - signs and seals the summons, keeps the property register, deals with copy applications. The Criminal Manual names the Sheristedar for the Metropolitan Magistrate's court, an office the BNSS no longer provides for; in the C.J.M. and J.M.F.C. courts the Clerk of the Court or the Senior Clerk does the same work.
roles.entry: Ministerial (judicial) establishment of the district judiciary, by recruitment and promotion.

roles.name: Nazir
roles.who: Keeps the court's cash, deposits and muddamal; prepares and signs the Property Register and verifies case property against the police Pavti or Yadi.
roles.entry: Ministerial establishment of the district judiciary.

roles.name: Bench Clerk / Board Clerk
roles.who: Runs the file through the hearing day, records the rojnama in CIS for the presiding officer to sign, and keeps each case's physical papers in a sealed, marked envelope. The Magistrate must nonetheless settle his own Board.
roles.entry: Ministerial establishment of the district judiciary.

roles.name: Stenographer
roles.who: Takes the magistrate's dictation of order sheets, online during or after the hearing in a SARAS court.
roles.entry: Ministerial establishment of the district judiciary.

roles.name: Video conferencing coordinator
roles.who: Runs the link at the court point and at the designated place, and counter-signs documents sent back from a remote point. Nominated by the High Court or the Principal District and Sessions Judge; the court may appoint any court official as the coordinator at the court point.
roles.entry: Nominated from the court's own staff or from the officials named in the rule 9 table for the place concerned.

story.summary: How a s.138 (cheque bounce, 'NACT') case runs in Haryana, end to end. It starts at the Panchkula lower-court filing window - submission, scrutiny, CIS entry and same-day dispatch to the trial court, from a June 2026 field interview with the filing assistants - and then follows the case through cognizance, the issue of summons or e-summons, appearance, the summary trial, the evidence, compounding, judgment and sentence, and appeal, grounded in Volume III of the Punjab and Haryana High Court's Rules and Orders and the High Court's E-Filing and Video Conferencing Rules.

roles.who: Receives the NACT file at the lower-court filing window, scrutinises it for completeness and attestation, enters it in the e-Courts CIS, assigns the NACT and CNR numbers, records it in the register and hands it to the peon for same-day dispatch.
roles.basis: Punjab & Haryana lower-court filing branch; described firsthand by the filing assistants (Panchkula, June 2026)

informal.practice: Some practices around the role are self-started and outside any rule - emailing a PDF copy of the file to an office inbox kept on the desktop, and parking the police station under 'offence remarks' for case distribution.

roles.who: The court's record-keeper and process clerk. He receives the file from the filing branch, registers the case in CIS once the objections are removed, and from then on owns the court's process - generating and publishing the summons and warrants, entering bail bonds and sureties in the module shared across Punjab and Haryana, attaching the service reports the process servers bring back, keeping the registers, binding and consigning the decided file to the record room, and assembling the monthly returns the High Court requires. He is distinct from the reader, who keeps the daily proceedings and the dates.
roles.basis: Rules and Orders Vol.III, Chapter 1 Part A and Chapter 11 Part A; described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (June 2026)

informal.practice: Several of the things this desk does every day rest on no rule: the cheque amount is typed into the CIS FIR field because there is no cheque-amount column (his own words: 'our own innovation, which is wrong'); surety process is sent from a blank template because CIS has no summons-to-surety form; the month's institution register is printed from e-Courts and pasted into the physical register; service reports are attached to files by hand, date by date; and the High Court's action plan and statements are built in a personal Excel workbook with VLOOKUP and date formulas, differently by every ahlmad.

roles.who: Carries the physical file the same day from the filing window to the destination court.
roles.basis: Court establishment; same-day dispatch in Panchkula

roles.who: Holds the CIS permission to release an e-filed case into the filing branch's queue. The assistants have no direct access and must telephone the computer room each time before they can edit and submit an e-filing. Two offices sit behind the local name and it is not settled which holds the permission: the Administrator whom E-Filing Rules r.3.2 appoints for e-filing matters, and the district court's own technical establishment, the System Officer and System Assistant who run the CIS server and its permissions at every court location.
roles.basis: Local CIS access-control arrangement, Panchkula district courts

informal.practice: An access bottleneck rather than a rule: e-filings can only be released by the computer room, so the filing branch phones it ten to fifteen times a day. Which office actually holds the release permission - the e-filing Administrator or the district System Officer - has not been established and is flagged for checking.

roles.who: The judicial magistrate who tries the NACT case. He examines the complainant on cognizance, decides between a summons and an e-summons, dispenses with the accused's personal attendance, holds the summary trial, and passes the judgment and sentence. Only a magistrate of the first class specially empowered, or a Bench so empowered, may hold a summary trial, which is the trial s.143 of the NI Act directs for a cheque case. He does not usually write the judgment himself: he dictates the arguments and the conclusion to the judgment writer in shorthand, in chambers after the court rises, and signs the transcript - every page of it, since it is not written in his own hand - and the judgment must be dated and signed at the time it is pronounced and cannot be altered afterwards except to correct a clerical error.
roles.basis: Rules and Orders Vol.III, Chapter 2 and Chapter 1 Parts B, C(i) and H

roles.who: The court's treasurer and custodian, whose office is the nazarat branch. The memorandum of the costs of witnesses is made out and forwarded to him for payment, and property sent in by the police is made over to him for custody. In a cheque case he is where a witness's diet and road money comes from, and where a fine or a deposit is lodged.
roles.basis: Rules and Orders Vol.III, Chapter 9 Part A and Chapter 11 Part E

roles.who: The officer who administers e-filing. For a district court he is the officer or official appointed by the District and Sessions Judge; for the High Court, the Registrar (IT) or an officer appointed by the Chief Justice. He releases and unlocks e-filed matters and transfers an action from a litigant in person to an advocate later engaged. This is the formal office behind what the Panchkula filing assistants call the computer room.
roles.basis: E-Filing Rules r.3.2, read with r.5

roles.who: The official who runs a video-conferenced hearing at each end. There is one at the Court Point and, where a witness or an accused is to be examined, one at the Remote Point as well, nominated by the High Court or the District Judge. Who it is depends on where the remote end sits - a consular official abroad, an official of another district court, the jail superintendent, a medical superintendent, or an officer of the legal services authority. He proves the identity of the person appearing and accounts for anyone else present at the Remote Point.
roles.basis: Video Conferencing Rules r.5, read with r.2(iii)

roles.who: The officer in charge of the police station, not below the rank of Sub-Inspector, under the Haryana Police Act. A cheque case generates no FIR and no investigation, so the police enter only once the court issues process: the station of the area serves the summons and executes any warrant the magistrate issues.
roles.basis: Haryana Police Act, 2007, ss.12 and 47, read with Vol.III r.1-Ci.6

roles.who: The technical official of a district court establishment. Each district has a System Officer and a System Assistant, and the district headquarters has a System Officer with two or three System Assistants depending on how many courts sit there. They run the CIS server and its performance, the hardware and the annual maintenance contract, and they are the first line for any software or hardware problem before it goes up to the High Court's IT wing. Data entry into CIS is not theirs: that is done by the court officials, the reader and the civil and criminal data entry staff.
roles.basis: District court technical establishment, Punjab, Haryana and U.T. Chandigarh; described firsthand by the High Court IT wing (June 2026). No rule in the corpus creates the post.

informal.title: the post is an establishment arrangement, not a creature of any rule in the corpus
informal.practice: The wing absorbs whatever court staff cannot handle - vendor and annual maintenance meetings, video conferencing, virtual inaugurations - on the working rule that anything with an 'e' or a 'computer' in it is forwarded to it.

roles.who: The official in each district court who generates the periodical statements and returns the High Court requires - cases registered, cases not registered and the reason, summonses issued, cases listed, cause lists and pendency by stage - and sends them up as soft copies. The duty is a rule: a magistrate exercising summary powers must prepare a monthly statement of the summary cases received and the progress in disposing of them, which reaches a s.138 case because it is triable summarily, and Volume III also speaks of quarterly statistical returns. The tool is local: the clerk works through the in-house Crystal CIS Reports application because CIS does not produce some of these reports usably.
roles.basis: Rules and Orders Volume III r.2.6 and r.11-A.15, read with NI Act §143

informal.practice: The reporting tool the clerk actually uses was built in-house by the High Court's technical wing, not supplied with CIS, and the High Court receives the returns as generated soft copies rather than querying the district data itself.

roles.who: Sits with the presiding judge, keeps the daily proceedings and the dates, and raises the objections on a newly filed case - court fee, condonation of delay - before it is registered. Those objections are argued before the judge and it is the judge who decides them. Volume III makes the reader responsible, when a holiday or an absence wipes out a day's list, for telling the parties and witnesses who turn up at a closed court what their fresh dates are.
roles.basis: Rules and Orders Vol.III, Chapter 1 Part A; described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (June 2026)

roles.who: Serves the court's summons and warrants and brings the served process back to the ahlmad, taking his receiving for it. Nothing of that return reaches the case record automatically: the ahlmad sorts the acknowledgments date by date and attaches them to each file by hand. Where the process has to be served outside the district it goes instead to the magistrate of that district, and where summons have gone out two or three times without result the judge sends the police, who are answerable to her.
roles.basis: Court ministerial establishment; described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (June 2026)

informal.practice: The whole return leg is manual. The server takes a receiving from the ahlmad, who then walks the acknowledgments into the files date by date; nothing about service status appears in the cause list or in CIS, so for process sent outside the district the court often learns of service only when the person appears.

roles.who: The desk that produces the written judgment. Once the judge has pronounced a file it comes to him, usually the next day, and he reads the whole proceeding from beginning to end before writing a word. He titles the file, logs into CIS for the template, the CNR number and the registration and institution dates, copies the cause title and the parties off the paper file, establishes who represented whom from the previous daily orders and the power of attorney at the back of the file, lifts the facts out of the complaint, records the proceedings and the evidence with their dates and exhibit numbers, takes the judge's dictation of the arguments and the conclusion in shorthand in chambers after the court rises, types the transcript the next day, and then uploads and e-signs it. He also keeps the conviction register and hands the convict his free copy, does the applications, and takes duty-magistrate work when the roster falls to his court. He is distinct from the stenographer outside the courtroom, who does the daily orders.
roles.basis: Rules and Orders Vol.III r.25-G.8 and Chapter 1 Part H, read with BNSS s.288(2) and s.392; the post and its daily content described firsthand by a judgment writer at the Panchkula district courts (June 2026)

informal.title: 'Judgment Writer' is a functional label on a stenographer-cadre post. No instrument in the corpus uses the title, or allocates daily orders to one stenographer and judgments to another - Volume III r.25-G.8 knows only 'stenographers'.
informal.practice: Much of the day rests on no rule: the facts of the complaint are retyped in full into every judgment even though the complaint has been on the file since it was filed; the conviction register is filled by copying details into MS Word, printing, cutting and pasting them into the paper book, a month at a time because daily entry is not possible; and a signed paper certificate goes to the main office each month saying all orders and judgments were uploaded, carrying no case numbers.

roles.who: The magistrate holding the duty roster, before whom work is put up that cannot wait for the court it belongs to. The month is divided among the judges of the establishment in blocks of a few days, and whatever arises for a court on leave goes to whoever is on duty - police remands, bail applications and miscellaneous applications. None of it is cheque-case work; it reaches the s.138 court and its staff through the roster, not the case type, and it is a real and unremarked call on the same people's time.
roles.basis: District court duty roster - court administration, created by no rule in this corpus; the remand work it carries is governed by Rules and Orders Vol.III r.11-B.9 and BNSS s.187. Described firsthand by a judgment writer at the Panchkula district courts (June 2026)

informal.title: The roster and its division of the month are establishment practice; no instrument in the corpus creates a 'duty magistrate'.

steps: The advocate submits the NACT file at the lower-court filing window (open until 12:00 PM); the filing assistant receives it.

The file is assembled in a fixed order: CIS proforma pasted on the cover and a second CIS proforma inside, then the index, the memo of parties, the application (the complaint, its 'prayer'), a Rs.10 court-fee ticket, an attested affidavit, the cheque (laminated), an attested power of attorney, and one full copy of the file per respondent.

The assistant scrutinises the file: CIS proforma pasted outside and present inside; index filled; pagination done; memo of parties carries address and phone; age recorded (treated as critical); every page signed and attested by the advocate for genuineness.
Mandatory supporting documents are checked - the cheque, the memo of parties and the legal notice - and the rest are verified against the list of documents in the index.

Limitation is checked; if the filing looks delayed the assistant tells the advocate verbally to attach a delay-condonation application (IA). The clerks use a rule of thumb of '45 days'; the statutory position is one month from the cause of action.

The assistant logs into the CIS module, opens the filing counter, chooses Criminal and then the NACT case type, and enters the complainant (name, age, mobile), the advocate, the opposite party and any extra-party count, the Rs.10 court fee and the Act (NI Act §138), then submits.
The system issues the NACT filing number and the CNR number (beginning HRPK for Panchkula), which are written on the file cover with the date.

There is no filing-counter field for the police station, so the jurisdictional station (taken from the bank where the cheque was presented) is parked under 'offence remarks' and used to distribute cases among the clerks. A s.138 case has no FIR, so the shared criminal template's FIR field does not apply.

The CIS instance the assistant is typing into is local. Each of the roughly 130 court locations in Punjab, Haryana and U.T. Chandigarh runs its own server, with a mirror alongside it for continuity, and the district's own System Officer and System Assistant administer it. Case data reflects in the National Judicial Data Grid in real time when the network is up, so a date the reader assigns is visible outside the court without anything being sent; orders and judgments are the exception and are uploaded each evening by running a command.

Nothing in the CIS screen can be changed locally. The core belongs to NIC and a High Court's suggestion moves only if the Supreme Court eCommittee approves it - days for a small change, otherwise the next version patch, which has meant years.
