So the mis-click risk between the civil and criminal columns, and the fields that do not fit a NACT case, are not local defects that a local fix can reach.
The entry is recorded in the physical register (NACT number, date, party names) and the file is carried the same day by a peon to the destination court.
The ahlmad receives the file in the court and takes over registration - entering the full address and extra-party details - and the subsequent process.

process.stage: 5 · Cognizance and the examination of the complainant
steps: The complaint is endorsed with the date of presentation the moment it is instituted, together with the name of the magistrate it is to go to, and the complainant is directed to appear for examination the same day or on one of the following days.

The first duty of the magistrate taking cognizance on the complaint is to examine the complainant, and any witnesses present, on oath, and to record the substance of that examination in writing, signed by the complainant, the witnesses and the magistrate.

Volume III insists that this examination is not a formality: it is what tells the magistrate whether to put the machinery of the criminal court in motion. If there is no sufficient ground for proceeding he dismisses the complaint at this stage.

In a cheque case the complainant's evidence is usually given on affidavit, which may be read in evidence at any stage, so the sworn statement, the cheque, the bank return memo and the demand notice do most of the work.

Jurisdiction is checked. Volume III puts the ordinary test at the place where the offence was committed, but for a cheque case s.142(2) of the NI Act displaces it with the branch of the bank where the payee maintains the account.

process.stage: 6 · Issue of process: summons, e-summons and the process fee
steps: Finding sufficient ground to proceed, the magistrate issues process for the attendance of the accused. No summons or warrant issues until a list of prosecution witnesses has been filed, and in a complaint case the process must be accompanied by a copy of the complaint.

Since the November 2018 amendment the magistrate may, in his discretion, issue a summons or an e-summons, and must record his reasons before issuing a warrant in a case where the law provides for a summons.

Where process fees are payable no process is to be issued until they are paid, and on default of payment within a reasonable time the magistrate may dismiss the complaint. This is the sharpest risk a cheque complainant carries immediately after cognizance.

Volume III also warns that great care should be taken not to issue a warrant where a summons would serve, since a warrant interferes with personal liberty, and that the court's discretion to make a warrant bailable should be used with regard to the nature of the offence and the position of the accused.

The process goes out for service through the police station of the area, whose Station House Officer is constituted by the Haryana Police Act; s.144 of the NI Act also allows a cheque summons to be served by speed post or an approved courier.
Where a witness is to be examined over a live link, the summons must state the date, time and venue of the Remote Point and direct him to attend there in person with proof of identity.

process.stage: 7 · Appearance, bail and dispensing with personal attendance
steps: A criminal trial is to be conducted in the presence of the accused, but the court has a discretion to dispense with his personal attendance and permit an advocate to appear for him. In a cheque case, where the accused is often out of station and the trial is meant to be summary, this is the everyday relief.

s.138 is a bailable offence. Volume III treats bail in a bailable case as a right and not a favour, tells the magistrate to fix the amount with regard to the social status of the accused and to see that it is not excessive, and reminds him that it is a hardship to detain an undertrial an hour longer than the law requires.
If the accused does not appear after service, or the court has reason to believe he has absconded or will not obey the summons, a warrant may issue in lieu of or in addition to the summons.

If he absconds, the court may proclaim him and attach his property as the last remedy for compelling attendance; Volume III warns that the procedure must be followed strictly or the attachment and sale will be set aside.

The accused may instead appear over a live link. Chapter 1 Part BB of Volume III makes the Video Conferencing Rules the procedure for criminal matters in the subordinate courts, a party or witness applies for remote appearance under r.6, and the court may frame the accusation and examine the accused by video conferencing.

When surety is offered for the accused, the person standing surety is entered in the High Court's in-house Surety module with an identity number, and checked against the courts of Punjab, Haryana and U.T. Chandigarh for whether he is a repeat or habitual surety. Someone who has already stood surety may stand again, but must produce a different document each time. This puts into software a declaration the law already requires: BNSS §486 makes every surety tell the court how many persons he has stood surety for, and §140 lets the Magistrate reject an unfit surety.

The concern behind the check is old. Rules and Orders Volume III r.10.9(9A), added in 2007, is aimed at the accused who absconds on a bogus surety or a bond furnished by a stock surety, and in the classes of case it covers requires two recent passport photographs plus one identity document, one photograph kept in the court record and one with the police station. By its own terms that requirement reaches NDPS cases, offences carrying more than ten years and special enactments, so it does not of its own force apply to a s.138 bail bond; the software check is applied more widely than the rule.

The check stops at the jurisdiction's edge. The surety database is centralised at the High Court and covers only Punjab, Haryana and U.T. Chandigarh, so a person standing surety repeatedly across state lines is invisible to it, and the declaration BNSS §486 asks for cannot be verified beyond one High Court.

process.stage: 8 · Summary trial: the accusation and the plea
steps: s.143 of the NI Act directs that a cheque case be tried summarily. Volume III Chapter 2 is the local manual for that trial: a summary trial may be held only by a magistrate of the first class empowered in that behalf, or by a Bench of magistrates so empowered.

The procedure followed at the hearing is that of a summons case, subject to the lighter record the summary chapters allow. The particulars of the offence are stated to the accused and he is asked whether he pleads guilty; no formal charge is framed in a summons case.

Volume III carries the general summary cap of three months' imprisonment, but s.143(1) of the NI Act lets a magistrate trying a cheque case summarily pass up to one year and a fine up to five thousand rupees. If a heavier sentence appears called for, the magistrate must recall the witnesses and rehear the case as a summons case.

If the accused pleads guilty the plea is recorded in his own words and he may be convicted on it; where he is not convicted the final order must show on its face whether he was discharged or acquitted.
The court may order the drawer to pay the complainant interim compensation of up to twenty per cent of the cheque amount while the trial runs.

In a summons case the record is ordinarily a memorandum of the substance of the evidence and no more. In a summary case in which no appeal lies no evidence need be recorded at all, only the prescribed particulars in the summary register; where an appeal does lie the magistrate must record the substance of the evidence and the particulars, and write a judgment before passing sentence.

Only relevant and admissible evidence should be recorded, an objection to admissibility should be decided forthwith with the objection and the decision written down, and the magistrate should note the demeanour of a witness where it is noteworthy.

Most of a cheque case is proved on paper: the complainant's evidence may be given on affidavit, the bank's slip is prima facie evidence of dishonour, and entries in bankers' books are proved by certified copy.
Evidence must be taken in the presence of the accused, or of his advocate where his personal attendance has been dispensed with.

A witness at a distance - typically the complainant or the bank official - may be examined from a Remote Point over a live link: identity proved first, oath administered, the deposition recorded and signed, and a document shown to him by transmitting its image between the Court Point and the Remote Point.

Once the examination of witnesses has begun the proceedings should continue from day to day, with reasons recorded for any adjournment beyond the following day. s.143(3) of the NI Act asks that the trial be concluded within six months of the filing of the complaint.
The accused is then examined on the circumstances appearing in the evidence against him; this too may be done over a video link.

process.stage: 10 · Dismissal in default and acquittal on the complainant's absence
steps: In a summons case instituted on a complaint, if the complainant fails to attend on a day fixed for hearing the accused should be acquitted, unless the magistrate adjourns the hearing or dispenses with the complainant's attendance and proceeds with the case.
Volume III opens this Part with the flat observation that some magistrates are inclined to dismiss cases in default hastily.

Before dismissing a case for the complainant's absence the magistrate must consider whether such an order is legal and whether it is justified by the circumstances, and reasons should always be recorded.

The complainant must have a full opportunity to appear: if he is absent when the case is first called it should be called again later, the time of dismissal must be noted on the record, and on tour a case is not to be dismissed unless he had due notice of the place of hearing.
A dismissal in default, or an acquittal that follows it, is challenged in revision - and the absence of recorded reasons is the usual ground on which a dismissed cheque complaint is revived.
Every offence punishable under the NI Act is compoundable, and most cheque cases end in a settlement rather than a verdict.

Compounding has the effect of an acquittal. No judgment on the facts is needed, but the statements of all the parties concerned must be recorded, and where the court's permission is required the reasons for granting it must be stated in the order directing the acquittal.

Volume III tells the magistrate to look at the facts before permitting a compromise, and in particular to ask whether it is a genuine reconciliation or the result of undue pressure on the complainant, and to record his reasons in every case in which he allows the parties to compromise.
A large share of cheque cases are settled in a Lok Adalat, whose award is final; parties may now take part in a Lok Adalat over a live link.

The judgment must contain the point or points for determination, the decision on them and the reasons for it, and on a conviction must indicate the offence and the sentence separately. Since a December 2021 amendment it must also carry the prescribed preface, a tabular statement of dates, and an appendix listing the witnesses, exhibits and material objects.

It is written in the language of the court or in English, pronounced in open court, and dated and signed at the time it is pronounced; the record and the final order must also disclose the criminal powers the officer exercised in deciding the case.

s.138 is punishable with imprisonment up to two years, or a fine up to twice the amount of the cheque, or both. Volume III's counterweight is that a fine, though the lightest punishment a court can impose, must never be excessive with reference to the means of the offender.

Imprisonment in default of payment may be ordered, but only within the limits the penal code sets, and it should be regulated with regard to the status of the accused so that he is induced to pay rather than to evade payment.

Where the fine is not paid at once the court may order it to be paid within a stated period or by instalments; an unpaid fine is realised on a warrant for levy, and compensation to the complainant is paid out of it.

A first offender may be released on probation instead of being sentenced. Volume III gives the Probation of Offenders Act a chapter of its own, on the premise that many offenders are weak characters rather than dangerous criminals and are better kept out of prison.

Who actually produces the document is a separate desk. The judge dictates the arguments and the conclusion; a judgment writer of the stenographer cadre assembles, types, uploads and e-signs the judgment, and the presiding officer signs every page of it. Stage 12a follows that work through.

A conviction by a magistrate is appealed to the Court of Session. Volume III requires the appellate court, once it decides to hear the appeal, to give notice of the day fixed for hearing to the appellant or his pleader.
A criminal appeal must be disposed of on its merits and cannot be dismissed in default - a point Volume III makes expressly to Sessions Judges.
The appellate court may order the appellant to deposit a minimum of twenty per cent of the fine or compensation awarded, while the appeal against a s.138 conviction is pending.

Orders that fall short of a conviction - a dismissal in default, an order on process fees, a refusal to dispense with attendance - are challenged in revision before the Sessions Judge or the High Court, whose power of superintendence over the subordinate courts is the source of these Rules and Orders themselves.

Digital copy by email: the advocate is asked to email a PDF of the file to an office inbox, which is kept unvalidated in a folder on the desktop - a recently self-started practice to pre-empt future e-filing and avoid re-scanning. Not required by any rule.

Cheque lamination: the cheque is laminated or kept in a polythene pouch purely for safety as it passes through many hands; it is explicitly not mandatory and its absence is not a ground to reject the file.

Google Translate as OCR: for civil suits (not NACT) with long relief text, the assistants photograph the pages and use Google Translate to copy and paste the text into CIS, to save typing under time pressure.

E-filing release: an e-filed case can only be released into the branch's queue by the computer room, so the assistants phone it repeatedly through the day; advocates often leave non-mandatory fields (the FIR number, the police station) blank, which the assistants then open the PDF to fill in.

Peripheral applications: because the CIS core cannot be changed by a High Court, anything the courts of Punjab and Haryana need for themselves is written in-house in PHP and run beside CIS, reading case data through an API and never writing back. Three exist - the Surety module, held centrally at the High Court, Crystal CIS Reports, held on each district's own server, and a third the technical wing named only as a s.138 tool and did not describe.

Local reporting: the monthly returns the High Court's branches require are generated district by district through Crystal CIS Reports, an in-house tool built because some CIS reports are not usable, and sent up as soft copies. The High Court does not query the district data itself for them, even though the network reaches every location.

Network headroom: the district courts share a Department of Justice wide-area network on a leased line with a small private address range, and some locations have no spare address at all. Anything new that has to be hosted for several courts is constrained first by that, before any question of software.

Cheque amount in the FIR field: with no cheque-amount column in the CIS criminal template, the ahlmad types the cheque amount into the FIR box so that the value can be read off the case record at a glance. His own verdict: 'this is some of our own innovation, which is wrong'. It is the same dead field the filing branch downstairs uses for the police station - a s.138 case has no FIR.

Blank-template surety process: CIS has no summons-to-surety form, so process to a surety is sent from a blank template. The statutory step behind it is real - the court must call on a person bound by a forfeited bond to pay the penalty or show cause - so the workaround is filling a genuine hole in the software, not inventing a step.
Register by print-and-paste: the month's institution report is run out of e-Courts, printed, and pasted into the physical register that Volume III requires the ahlmad to keep.

Manual service tracking: process servers take the ahlmad's receiving for served process, and he attaches the acknowledgments to each file by hand, date by date, because no service status reaches the cause list or the case record.

Personal Excel returns: the High Court's action plan and its twenty to thirty statements are rebuilt by each ahlmad in his own spreadsheet with VLOOKUP and date formulas, because CIS gives pendency but not disposal and its reports are not aligned with the High Court's format. Explicitly informal, unversioned and untrained - the same shape of private artefact HR-01 found at the filing window.

Conviction register by cut-and-paste: the conviction details are copied out of the judgment into MS Word, shortened, printed, cut and pasted into the physical conviction register, and a whole month is done in a day or two at month end because daily entry is not possible. The register is not on CIS. It is the same print-and-paste answer the ahlmad's desk uses for the institution register, but with no database behind it.

Retyping the complaint: the facts of the complaint are typed out again in full into every judgment, months after the same complaint was captured at the filing window. The judgment writer, asked twice whether anything he does is repetitive enough to be taken off him, named this and nothing else - and said that if the complaint were digitised at scanning, the judgment would come down to the arguments and the operative part, with the evidence a further candidate since it is complete by the time the file reaches him.

The blanket upload certificate: around the third of each month a signed paper certificate goes down to the main office saying that for the previous month all orders and judgments have been uploaded. It carries no case numbers and no counts, while CIS already reports which orders are pending upload - a monthly assurance that could be computed rather than certified.

process.stage: 4a · The ahlmad's desk: objections, registration and numbering
steps: The file arrives from the filing branch with its filing number. The reader of the court raises the objections on it - court fee, condonation of delay - and those are argued before the judge, who decides them. Condonation is squarely judicial: the complaint must be made within one month of the cause of action, and only the court may take cognizance later on sufficient cause.

Once the objections are removed and registration is permitted, the ahlmad registers the case in CIS and the main case number issues. Volume III's standing requirement is that a summary case be entered in Register No. 1 as soon as it is received in court, and it makes the ahlmad the keeper of the court's registers.

He enters the complainant and his advocate, then several addresses for the accused. There is no cheque-amount column in the criminal template, so the cheque amount is typed into the FIR field - a self-started local convention he himself calls wrong. A s.138 case has no FIR at all, and the filing branch downstairs uses the same dead field for the police station.

The file then goes to the reader for the next date, the preliminary evidence is taken and the exhibits go on, and the summoning order follows on the same day. The advocate supplies the copies of the complaint that must go out with the process.

process.stage: 6a · Process generation, service and the coercive ladder
steps: The ahlmad opens process generation in CIS, selects the court and the date, and picks the process from a numbered list. A s.138 case has its own template - 'summons to accused in 138' - which prints differently from the ordinary summons; s.144 of the NI Act gives the cheque summons its own service regime by speed post or approved courier, and since November 2018 Volume III lets the magistrate issue it as an e-summons.

The document prints 'Draft' in large letters until it is published; a draft is not acceptable for use. That is not a formality - a summons must be signed by the presiding officer and bear the seal of the court, or bear the image of the seal or a digital signature if electronic, and a warrant must likewise be signed and sealed.

If the accused appears, his bail bond and the names of his sureties go into a module shared across the Punjab and Haryana establishments, so that one person cannot quietly stand surety in case after case. That is the software form of the surety's statutory declaration of how many persons he has stood surety for, and of Volume III's photograph-and-identity requirement against the stock surety. There is no summons-to-surety form in the module, so surety process is sent from a blank template.

If he does not appear the ladder runs bailable warrant, then non-bailable warrant, then a request to the bank for the KYC address on the account (the address the complainant gave may be false), then fresh warrants at the address the bank returns, then proclamation, then attachment of the property the complainant's advocate lists. Volume III still cites the 1898 numbering here; the live provisions are BNSS §§90, 84 and 85.

Attachment is often spoken of at the desk as a way of getting the cheque amount paid. It is not. Volume III calls it the last remedy for compelling attendance, the attached property remains at the disposal of Government, and it goes back to the absconder if he appears within two years. The complainant's money comes instead from compensation out of a fine, or from a settlement.

Process for another district is sent to the magistrate of that district, who has it served and returns it with proof of service; out of state, the police travel, get the warrant endorsed at the local police station and execute it from that jurisdiction. A warrant of arrest may be executed anywhere in India.

The return leg is entirely manual. Process servers bring the served process back and take the ahlmad's receiving; he sorts the acknowledgments date by date and attaches them to each file by hand. Nothing about service status shows in the cause list or in the issuing court's CIS record, so for process sent outside the district the court often learns of service only when the person appears. The Sanhita already contemplates a service register with address, email and phone.

process.stage: 13a · Consignment, the record room and the miscellaneous file
steps: After judgment the file comes back to the ahlmad. He binds it, generates the 'Index for Decided File' proforma out of CIS - the same report can be produced for a pending file - and sends it down to the record room. Volume III's requirement is that the record be complete before it is consigned.

A criminal miscellaneous matter arising out of a decided and consigned NACT file is separated from it and becomes a fresh file with its own number, obtained from the filing branch downstairs. Volume III states the same principle for transfer applications: a separate record, separately consigned.
The record-room rules themselves - retention periods, indexing, destruction - sit in Rules and Orders Volumes IV and VI-B, which are not yet in this corpus.

process.stage: 13b · Registers, returns and the High Court action plan
steps: The registers are the ahlmad's charge. A summary case must be entered in Register No. 1 as soon as it is received in court and again in the register of summary cases when the accused appears, and the presiding officer must inspect the registers monthly. In Panchkula the paper register is now fed from the database: the month's institution report is run out of e-Courts for the establishment and case type, printed, and pasted in.

The reporting stack above it is formal and heavy. Every judicial officer must send the High Court a monthly statement of criminal cases pending over one year in the prescribed proforma before the 10th of the following month, with history sheets for the six oldest; daily progress reports are prescribed besides; and a monthly statement of summary cases received and disposed of is required on top.

In practice the High Court asks for some twenty to thirty statements, including an 'action plan' list of two hundred cases kept updated almost daily out of a pendency of about a thousand. CIS produces a management report, a balance sheet and the goshwara, but its output is not aligned with the format the High Court asks for, and it returns pendency without disposal - so age at disposal has to be computed from the institution and decision dates by hand.

The gap is closed with a personal spreadsheet. The ahlmad exports the case data, and rebuilds the statements in Excel with VLOOKUP and date formulas on an Ubuntu desktop. He is explicit that this is not formal and that every ahlmad has his own way of doing it, and that he has had no training in it. His ask is the simplest one in the interview: make the system report what the High Court asks for.

process.stage: 12a · Writing the judgment: dictation, transcript and upload
steps: The judgment is not written by the judge's own hand. It is prepared by the judgment writer, a stenographer-cadre desk inside the court, and signed by the presiding officer - every page of it, because it was not written by him. Volume III has recognised this since long before CIS, and for a summary trial BNSS goes further: the High Court may authorise the record or the judgment, or both, to be prepared by an officer appointed for the purpose, the magistrate signing what is prepared.

The file reaches the writer after pronouncement, usually the next day, and he reads the whole proceeding from start to end before writing. He assembles the document in a fixed order: title, then CIS for the template, the CNR number and the registration and institution dates, then the cause title and the parties off the paper file, then the appearances, then the facts out of the complaint, then the proceedings - summons, notice of accusation, plea of defence, evidence - and last the arguments and the conclusion. No rule prescribes that order; what the rules prescribe is the shape of the finished thing.

That shape is exact. Since correction slip no.40 of December 2021 every judgment must open with a preface naming the parties in FORM A, carry a tabular statement of dates in FORM B, and close with an appendix listing the witnesses, the exhibits and the material objects in FORM C, referring to each by number and not only by name; and it must state the point or points for determination, the decision and the reasons, and on conviction the offence and the punishment separately.

So the writer's day goes on recovering exact data from paper: the summons date, the date of the notice of accusation, what the complainant tendered and under which exhibit number, the date evidence was closed. BNSS fixes the particulars a summary record must carry, and Volume III requires the substance of the evidence in a summary case that is appealable, which a cheque case is. A wrong cheque number, address or advocate in the judgment is treated at the desk as unfixable, and the Sanhita agrees: once signed, a judgment cannot be altered except to correct a clerical or arithmetical error.

Who represented whom is read back off the previous daily orders and cross-checked against the power of attorney pinned at the back of the file, page by page. Nothing about appearance is queryable, so the whole check is manual - and the daily orders themselves belong to a different desk, the stenographer outside the courtroom who does the daily orders while this desk does the judgments.

The judge dictates the arguments and the conclusion; the writer takes it in shorthand, in chambers after the court has risen, and types it the following day. This is the route the Sanhita itself lays down for a judgment delivered in full - taken down in shorthand, the transcript signed page by page as soon as it is ready and marked with the date of delivery in open court. Volume III adds only that judgments are not to be written at home during court hours.

The typed judgment is uploaded to CIS and e-signed with a digital signature held on a pen-drive token. Orders can be uploaded in a batch, but each still has to be selected one at a time, and there is no bulk download. The writer also runs the CIS reporting to see which of his own orders are still pending upload, and around the third of each month signs a paper certificate for the main office saying that for the previous month all orders and judgments have been uploaded - a single format with no case numbers and no counts on it.

The workload behind all this, as reported: two or three judgments a day, about an hour for a simple file and considerably longer for one with lengthy cross-examination and many documents, and about fifteen pages to a judgment. Almost nothing repeats between judgments except the conclusion, some standard sentences and two or three authorities in the observations. The same desk also takes the applications and, when the roster falls to its court, duty-magistrate work - police remands and bail applications, none of it cheque-case work.

process.stage: 12b · The free copy and the conviction register
steps: On a conviction the accused gets a copy of the judgment free of cost, so that he can appeal. Volume III requires it soon after delivery wherever the accused is sentenced to imprisonment, and the Sanhita says the same immediately after pronouncement; where the judgment is appealable but no imprisonment is passed - the ordinary s.138 outcome of fine and compensation - the free certified copy comes on the accused's application. At Panchkula it is treated as a right that needs no request.

It is handed over the same day, on the footing that the convict is physically present for the pronouncement. That holds most of the time but not always: Volume III itself allows the accused to be absent at pronouncement where his attendance has been dispensed with and the sentence is one of fine only.

The copy is what makes the appeal possible. A petition of appeal must be accompanied by a copy of the judgment appealed against, and Volume III works the free supply out for appeals and revisions, including for summons cases where the accused is in jail.

The handover is acknowledged in a physical conviction register: the convict signs 'copy received' in the corner, and against it the entry carries the case and registration number, the accused's name, the sentence and the compensation or fine - the same figures Volume III requires to be settled with regard to the offender's means. The register itself is prescribed outside Volume III, in the Rules and Orders volumes that hold the numbered criminal registers and are not yet in this corpus; Volume III's own conviction-reporting duty covers a listed set of Penal Code and special-Act offences and does not reach the NI Act.

It used to be handwritten. It now runs on a workaround: the details are copied out of the judgment into MS Word, shortened, printed, cut and pasted into the paper register, and because daily entry is impossible a whole month is done in a day or two at the end of the month. The register is not held in CIS at all, so the acknowledgment taken on the day of conviction and the entry recording it are made weeks apart.

vocabulary.gloss: The filing-branch clerk who receives a s.138 (NACT) file at the lower-court filing window, checks it for completeness and attestation, enters it in the e-Courts CIS, assigns the NACT filing number and CNR number, records it in the register and hands it to the peon for same-day dispatch to the trial court. A formal court-staff role; some of the practices around it (an emailed PDF copy, parking the police station under 'offence remarks') are self-started and outside any rule.
vocabulary.source: Punjab & Haryana lower-court filing branch; described by the filing assistants, Panchkula (PUCAR field interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The record-keeper and process clerk of a criminal court. He receives the file from the filing branch once it has a filing number, registers the case in CIS after the objections are removed and the main case number issues, enters the parties and addresses, and from then on owns the court's process: generating and publishing summons and warrants, entering bail bonds and sureties, attaching the service reports the process servers bring back, keeping the registers, binding and consigning the decided file, and building the monthly returns the High Court asks for. Volume III recognises the office directly - talbana and stamped postal envelopes filed by litigants are received by the ahlmad or the moharrir against a receipt and never by any other member of the ministerial establishment, and the registers of a magistrate's court are maintained by the ahlmad attached to it. He is not the reader: Volume III names the reader of the court separately, and at Panchkula the reader raises the objections and keeps the dates while the ahlmad registers, generates process and keeps the record.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.4 and rule 11-A.14; described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The office that holds the CIS permission to release ('consume' or approve) an e-filed case into the filing branch's queue. The filing assistants have no direct access, so they telephone the computer room each time an e-filing arrives - often ten to fifteen times a day - before they can edit and submit it. 'Computer room' is the local name, and two different offices sit behind it. The E-Filing Rules create the Administrator, who for a district court is the officer appointed by the District and Sessions Judge, for everything connected with e-filing. Separately, every court location has its own technical establishment - a System Officer and a System Assistant - who run the CIS server and its permissions and who are very probably the people the branch actually rings. Which of the two holds the release permission has not been established. An access-control chokepoint rather than a rule.
vocabulary.source: Local CIS access arrangement, Panchkula district courts (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The Case Information System - the national e-Courts case-management software the court works in from filing to judgment. The filing assistant logs in, opens the filing counter, chooses Criminal and then the NACT case type, and enters the party, court-fee and Act details; the system then issues the case numbers. A known pain point is that civil and criminal columns appear together, inviting mis-clicks. At the far end of the case the judgment writer logs in to lift the judgment template, the CNR number and the registration and institution dates, then uploads and e-signs the judgment and runs the reporting that shows which of his orders are still pending upload; orders can be uploaded in a batch but each has to be selected one at a time, and there is no bulk download. It belongs to NIC, not to the High Court: the versions reported were 1.0 from 2011, 2.0 from 2014, 3.0 from 2017 and 4.0 from 2025, and each district court location runs its own instance on its own server, syncing case data to the NJDG in real time while orders and judgments are pushed each evening. A High Court cannot change the core - a suggestion goes to NIC and moves only if the Supreme Court eCommittee approves - so anything a court needs for itself is built beside CIS as a read-only peripheral application.
vocabulary.source: e-Courts Project, Supreme Court e-Committee - Case Information System (CIS)

vocabulary.gloss: The Case Number Record - a nationally unique 16-character identifier the e-Courts system assigns to every case, used to track and search it across courts. In Panchkula the CNR begins 'HRPK' (Haryana, Panchkula). The filing assistant writes it on the file cover alongside the NACT number.
vocabulary.source: e-Courts Project - CNR (Case Number Record), the nationally unique case identifier

vocabulary.gloss: The filing number the CIS generates for a Negotiable Instruments Act case. 'NACT' is the e-Courts case-type code for a s.138 cheque-bounce complaint; selecting it under Criminal and submitting the party and Act details produces the NACT number, which is written on the file cover.
vocabulary.source: e-Courts CIS case-type code for Negotiable Instruments Act s.138 complaints (NACT)

vocabulary.gloss: The list of the parties to the case - the complainant and each respondent with their address and phone number - filed as part of the complaint set. It is a mandatory, scrutinised document; the filing assistant checks that the address and phone fields are present because they are needed for service and registration.
vocabulary.source: Standard pleading in the filed set; scrutinised at the filing window (Panchkula, PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: A free-text field in the CIS filing form that the assistants use to park the jurisdictional police station, because the filing counter has no dedicated column for it. The police station is derived from the bank where the cheque was presented and is used to distribute NACT cases among the clerks - not for any investigation, since a s.138 case has no FIR.
vocabulary.source: Local CIS data-entry practice, Panchkula filing branch (PUCAR interview, June 2026) - a workaround for a missing field

vocabulary.gloss: The lower-court counter where advocates submit physical NACT files and the filing assistant receives, scrutinises and enters them. In Panchkula the window is open until 12:00 PM and files are processed the same day; it handles 40 to 50 files of all categories a day, of which up to about 10 are NACT. It is the modern form of the Volume III petition box, and it sits beside the designated counters and e-Service Centres at which the same complaint may be filed electronically. Court and office timings across the subordinate courts of Haryana are fixed by rule: court from 10:00 to 16:30, office from 09:30 to 17:00.
vocabulary.source: Panchkula district courts filing branch (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The Punjab and Haryana High Court's standing instructions to the subordinate criminal courts of Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh - the Haryana counterpart of Kerala's Criminal Rules of Practice. Volume III governs the whole spine of a cheque case: cognizance on a complaint, the issue of process, the conduct of the trial, the record of evidence, dismissal in default, the judgment, the sentence and the appeal. It is made under the High Court's powers of superintendence in Articles 225 and 227 of the Constitution, and it opens at Chapter 1 Part A with the uniform court and office timings for every subordinate court in the two States. It still cites the old Codes of 1898 and 1973 by their former section numbers, so it has to be read through the 2024 Sanhita mapping.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.1

vocabulary.gloss: The first duty of a magistrate taking cognizance on a complaint: to examine the complainant, and any witnesses present, on oath and to record the substance of that examination in writing, signed by the complainant, the witnesses and the magistrate. Volume III insists it is not a formality - it is what tells the magistrate whether to put the machinery of the criminal court in motion or to dismiss the complaint for want of sufficient ground. In a cheque case this is the moment the complaint becomes a case, and in practice the s.145 affidavit does much of the work.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-B.4

vocabulary.gloss: An electronic summons. Since the November 2018 amendment to Volume III a magistrate may, in his discretion, issue a summons or an e-summons for the attendance of the accused, and must record his reasons before issuing a warrant in a case where the law provides for a summons. It is the Haryana rule-level recognition of electronic process, and it sits alongside s.144 of the NI Act, which lets a cheque summons go by speed post or an approved courier.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-Ci.2

vocabulary.gloss: The fee payable for issuing and serving the court's process. Volume III is blunt about it: where process fees or other fees are payable, no process is to be issued until they are paid, and on default of payment within a reasonable time the magistrate may dismiss the complaint. It is the sharpest early risk a cheque complainant carries after cognizance, and it is separate from the ten rupee court fee on the complaint itself. In the Punjab and Haryana courts the process money handed in with stamped postal envelopes is called talbana.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-Ci.2

vocabulary.gloss: A box placed in the verandah of the court house about an hour before the court sits, into which petitions and applications are dropped. It is opened in the magistrate's presence about fifteen minutes after the court opens, again before the lunch recess and a third time fifteen minutes before rising, and every petition in it is initialled by him. Members of the ministerial establishment are forbidden to receive complaints or petitions directly from lawyers or their clerks. It is the Volume III answer to the counter queue, and the rule-level ancestor of the Panchkula filing window.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.4

vocabulary.gloss: The office note or report put up to the magistrate on a petition before he can pass orders on it. Volume III has the magistrate either pass proper orders on a petition forthwith or tell the petitioner when the orders will be ready, once the necessary kaifiyats have been put up. It is one of the Urdu-derived establishment words that the Punjab and Haryana courts still run on, alongside ahlmad, nazir, peshi and talbana.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.4

vocabulary.gloss: The register in which the dates of hearing of the cases before a court are entered. Volume III makes the presiding officer himself fix fresh dates in the peshi register when an unexpected holiday or absence wipes out a day's list, and then hand the register to the reader of the court, who is responsible for telling the parties and witnesses who turn up at a closed court what their new date is. It is the paper ancestor of the CIS cause list, and 'peshi' remains the everyday word for a date of appearance in a Haryana court.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.10

vocabulary.gloss: The direction that once the examination of witnesses has begun the proceedings continue from day to day until the witnesses in attendance have been examined, with reasons recorded in writing for any adjournment beyond the following day. Volume III repeats it twice, for speedy disposal generally and for the stage after the accusation is put. It is the local counterpart of s.143(3) of the NI Act, which asks that a cheque trial be concluded within six months of the filing of the complaint, and the standard against which the years a NACT case actually takes are measured.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-D.11

vocabulary.gloss: The lighter record a summons case and a summary trial get. In a summons case the record is ordinarily a memorandum of the substance of the evidence and no more; in a summary case in which no appeal lies no evidence need be recorded at all, only the prescribed particulars in the summary register, but where an appeal does lie the magistrate must record the substance of the evidence and the particulars, and write a judgment before passing sentence. Since a cheque case is tried summarily and carries an appeal, this is the shape of the trial record a s.138 file actually ends up with. It is also what the judgment writer has to reconstruct from the file: what the complainant tendered, under which exhibit number, and the date on which the evidence was closed - Volume III r.1-H.1(i-b) requires exhibits to be referred to by their number and not only by name, and BNSS s.286 lists the particulars a summary record must carry.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-E.8
aka: memorandum of the substance of the evidence

vocabulary.gloss: Dismissal of a complaint case because the complainant did not appear. Volume III opens the chapter with the warning that some magistrates are inclined to dismiss cases in default hastily, and then requires the magistrate to consider whether such an order is legal and whether it is justified by the circumstances, and to record his reasons in every case. A complainant absent when the case is first called must have it called again later, and the time of dismissal must be noted on the record. This is the check a dismissed cheque complaint is revived on, in revision.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-F.2
aka: dismissal for absence of the complainant

vocabulary.gloss: In a summons case instituted on a complaint, if the complainant fails to attend on a day fixed for hearing the accused is to be acquitted, unless the magistrate adjourns the hearing or dispenses with the complainant's attendance and proceeds. A s.138 case is tried as a summons case, so this is not a mere dismissal - the accused walks free on the merits, and the complainant's remedy is revision, not a fresh complaint. It is the procedural risk the complainant carries on every single date.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-D.5
aka: acquittal for non-appearance of the complainant

vocabulary.gloss: The Volume III rule that a fine, though the lightest punishment a criminal court can impose, must never be excessive with reference to the means of the offender. Indiscriminate fines only waste the time of the courts and the police in trying to realise them and harass the convict and his dependants. On a s.138 conviction the fine may run to twice the amount of the cheque, so this is the state-level counterweight a Haryana magistrate applies when fixing it, and the reason the sentence in default is set with the status of the accused in mind.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 19-B.1
aka: fine in proportion to the offender's means
capacity of the convict to pay

vocabulary.gloss: Imprisonment ordered to be served if the fine is not paid. Volume III confirms that criminal courts are empowered to impose it but only subject to the limits the penal code sets, and asks that it be regulated with regard to the status of the accused so that he is induced to pay rather than to evade payment. In a cheque case, where the fine can be twice the cheque amount, the default sentence is often the only thing that actually moves money.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 19-B.2
aka: imprisonment in default of payment of fine

vocabulary.gloss: Where an offender is sentenced to a fine and to imprisonment in default and does not pay at once, the court may order that the fine be paid within a stated period or by instalments. Volume III points the magistrate at the power expressly. In a s.138 case this is the ordinary route by which a convicted drawer pays the cheque amount over to the complainant without going to jail, and it is the sentencing side of the settlements that end most cheque cases.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 19-B.3
aka: postponement of realisation of the fine

vocabulary.gloss: The court's treasurer and custodian. The nazir holds cash and property in the court's keeping, and pays out the money side of a case: the memorandum of the costs of witnesses is made out and forwarded to him, and property sent in by the police is made over to him for custody. The office is the nazarat branch. In a cheque case the nazir is who a witness's diet and road money comes from, and where a fine or a deposit is lodged.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 9-A.3

vocabulary.gloss: The daily allowance, with road money, paid to a witness who attends a criminal court. Volume III sets out when the court pays these expenses and carries a whole set of State instructions written for the nazarat officers and the presiding officers to prevent fraud and embezzlement in their disbursement. In a cheque case they are what the bank official who proves the return memo is entitled to, and one of the practical reasons a bank witness is better examined over a live link.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 9-B.1

vocabulary.gloss: The officer who administers e-filing. Under the E-Filing Rules the Administrator is, for the High Court, the Registrar (IT) or an officer appointed by the Chief Justice, and for a district court the officer or official appointed by the District and Sessions Judge. Everything that has to be unlocked in an e-filed case goes through him, including transferring an action from a litigant in person to the advocate later engaged. This is the formal name for the office the Panchkula filing assistants call the computer room and telephone before an e-filed NACT case can be released into their queue.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 3.2

vocabulary.gloss: The defined term that decides whether the e-filing regime reaches a cheque case at all. An Action under the E-Filing Rules includes all proceedings instituted in the court or tribunal, and criminal complaints are named expressly, alongside suits, petitions, appeals, revisions and interlocutory applications. So a s.138 complaint is inside the e-filing rules and not merely a civil-side facility, and every rule that follows - formatting, digital signature, court fees, retention of originals, computation of time - applies to it.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 3.1

vocabulary.gloss: A counter at which a case can be filed electronically over the court's intranet instead of over the internet, together with the e-Service Centres provided for the purpose. The E-Filing Rules apply to both online e-filing and e-filing through designated counters, and filing at a counter is permitted up to 1600 hours on a court working day. For a filer who has no digital signature, or whose document will not scan, this is the staffed alternative to the portal - and the point at which the e-filing regime meets the physical filing window.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2

vocabulary.gloss: The date on which an action is treated as filed electronically: the date it is received in the Registry within the prescribed time on a working day, reckoned in Indian Standard Time. Online filing after midnight counts as the next day, and filing on a gazetted holiday or a day the court is closed counts as the next working day; failure of the portal is no ground for exemption from limitation. Limitation is otherwise the same regime as physical filing. This is what fixes whether a cheque complaint is inside the one month allowed by s.142(1)(b) of the NI Act.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 15

vocabulary.gloss: The duty on a party who e-files scanned documents to keep the originals for production or inspection as the court directs, to preserve a signed vakalatnama or an attested affidavit for at least two years after final disposal including appeal, and to bear the burden of producing the originals and proving they are genuine. Some documents must be kept permanently - and a negotiable instrument is one of them, except a cheque. So the cheque, which is the whole of a s.138 case, sits under the ordinary rule and has to be produced when the court calls for it.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 11

vocabulary.gloss: The form an e-filed document has to take. All original typed material must be prepared as the Rules and Orders require and converted into an optical-character-recognition searchable PDF, and documents that are not text - scans, photographs - must be scanned to the stated standard. It is the bar the cheque, the bank return memo and the demand notice have to clear before an e-filed cheque complaint will be accepted, and the reason the Panchkula assistants ask for a clean PDF copy of a physical file.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 7

vocabulary.gloss: A live television link or other audio-video electronic arrangement by which a person who is physically absent from the courtroom is nevertheless virtually present in it, to give evidence and be cross-examined. The Video Conferencing Rules make video conferencing available at all stages of a judicial proceeding and treat a proceeding conducted that way as a judicial proceeding for every purpose, using the software the High Court designates. Chapter 1 Part BB of Volume III is what carries these Rules into the criminal courts where a cheque case is tried.
vocabulary.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(ix)

vocabulary.gloss: The courtroom, or any place where the court is physically convened, in a hearing held over a live link - including the place where a commissioner or an inquiring officer holds proceedings on the court's directions. It is the anchor end of a video-conferenced hearing: the judge, the record and the coordinator who runs the link sit at the Court Point, and a document at the Court Point is shown to a remote witness by transmitting an image of it.
vocabulary.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(v)

vocabulary.gloss: The place where a person appears or is examined through a video link. It may be another court, a legal services authority or mediation centre, a jail, a hospital, or an Indian consulate abroad, and the Rules name who acts as coordinator at each. A summons to a witness who is to be examined by video conferencing must state the date, time and venue of the Remote Point and direct him to attend there in person with proof of identity. In a cheque case this is usually where the out-of-station complainant or the bank official appears from.
vocabulary.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(x)

vocabulary.gloss: The defined class of people who may take part in a hearing over a live link: the person to be examined, the person in whose presence proceedings are to be recorded, an advocate or a party in person who intends to examine a witness, anyone required to make submissions, and anyone else the court permits to appear by video conferencing. In a s.138 case it covers the complainant, the accused whose personal attendance has been dispensed with, and the bank witness.
vocabulary.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 2(xii)

vocabulary.gloss: The official who runs a video-conferenced hearing at each end. There is a coordinator at the Court Point and, where a witness or an accused is to be examined, one at the Remote Point as well; in the district judiciary they are nominated by the High Court or the District Judge. Who it is depends on where the remote end sits - a consular official abroad, a nominated official of another district court, the jail superintendent, a medical superintendent, or an officer of the legal services authority. The coordinator identifies the person appearing, and identifies and accounts for anyone else present at the Remote Point.
vocabulary.source: Rules for Video Conferencing for Courts, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 5

vocabulary.gloss: A piece of software a High Court or district court builds for itself alongside CIS, because the CIS core cannot be changed locally. A peripheral application reads case data through an API - case type, case status, case number, party name - and cannot write anything back into CIS. Punjab and Haryana runs three of them, written in-house in PHP: the Surety module, Crystal CIS Reports and a s.138 tool. The read-only limit is the boundary any court-facing system has to design around: it can show and cross-check what CIS holds, but the case record itself is only ever written inside CIS.
vocabulary.source: e-Courts CIS architecture as described by the IT wing of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The in-house application in which a person offering surety for an accused is recorded, with an Aadhaar number, and checked against every other court in Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh to see whether he is a repeat or habitual surety. A person who has already stood surety may stand again, but must produce a different document each time - a motorcycle registration certificate, then a car registration certificate, then a mortgage of property. It puts into software the declaration BNSS §486 already requires of every surety and the stock-surety concern behind Rules and Orders Volume III r.10.9. The database sits centrally at the High Court; it cannot see any other state, so a surety standing repeatedly across state lines is invisible to it.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders, Volume III, rule 10.9 (surety and identity documents), read with BNSS §486; the module itself described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: A person who stands surety again and again, for strangers and for a consideration, rather than out of any real connection with the accused. Rules and Orders Volume III r.10.9(9A) was added in 2007 to stop accused persons absconding on a bogus surety or a bond furnished by a stock surety: in the classes of case it covers, the surety must give two passport photographs no more than six months old, one kept in the court record and one with the police station, together with a passport, election identity card, PAN card, bank card, government identity card or any other document ordinarily issued after verification of identity and address. BNSS §486 goes wider and makes every surety declare how many people he has already stood surety for.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders, Volume III, rule 10.9(9A) (added 2007), read with BNSS §486 and §140

vocabulary.gloss: CCR, the reporting application the High Court's technical wing built in-house because some of the reports CIS produces are not usable. It runs on each district's own server, since it can only read that district's local CIS data, and the Statement Clerk uses it to produce the monthly returns the High Court's branches ask for - cases registered, cases not registered and the reason, summonses issued, cases listed, cause lists, pendency by stage, and how many cases moved from one court to another on a given date, in a single click.
vocabulary.source: In-house peripheral application of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana, described by its IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The official posted in each district court who generates the periodical statements and returns the High Court requires - what was registered, what was not and why, what was listed, what is pending and at which stage. The duty is old: Rules and Orders Volume III r.2.6 makes a magistrate exercising summary powers prepare a statement every month of the summary cases received and the progress in disposing of them, which reaches cheque cases because NI Act §143 makes a s.138 complaint triable summarily, and r.11-A.15 speaks of quarterly statistical returns and of the records the statistical writer needs to make them out. In practice the clerk now produces them through the in-house Crystal CIS Reports tool and sends soft copies up.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders, Volume III, rules 2.6 and 11-A.15 (periodical statements and statistical returns); the post described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The technical official posted in a district court establishment. There is a System Officer and a System Assistant per district, and at the district headquarters a System Officer with two or three System Assistants depending on how many courts sit there. They run the CIS server and its performance, the hardware and the annual maintenance contract, while the court officials do the data entry. No rule in the corpus creates the post, and it is not the same as the Administrator whom E-Filing Rules r.3.2 appoints for e-filing matters, although this is very probably the office a filing branch means when it says it has to telephone 'the computer room'.
vocabulary.source: District court technical establishment, Punjab and Haryana; described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026). No rule in the corpus creates the post.

vocabulary.gloss: The National Judicial Data Grid, the national store into which every court's case data flows. Each of the district court servers in Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh talks to it directly over whitelisted addresses. Case data reflects in it in real time when the network is up, so a date the reader assigns appears without anything being sent; orders and judgments are the exception and are pushed each evening by running a command.
vocabulary.source: e-Courts Project, Supreme Court eCommittee - National Judicial Data Grid; the local synchronisation described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The National Informatics Centre, which builds and maintains CIS for the courts. A High Court can suggest a change but cannot make one: the suggestion goes to NIC's Pune unit, which acts only after the Supreme Court eCommittee approves it. A small change may be done in a few days; otherwise it waits for the next version patch, into which suggestions from every High Court in India are gathered. NIC also supplies the migration script that moves a court's data from one CIS version to the next, and NIC scientists are posted at the High Court itself.
vocabulary.source: National Informatics Centre, the technical agency for the e-Courts project; its role described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The e-Committee of the Supreme Court of India, which governs the e-Courts project and is the gate every change to CIS has to pass. A High Court's suggestion reaches NIC, but NIC only builds it once the eCommittee agrees; if it does not, the suggestion waits for the next version, and that has meant years. This is why a court that needs something now builds a peripheral application instead of asking for the core to change.
vocabulary.source: e-Committee of the Supreme Court of India, the governing body of the e-Courts project; its role in the change route described by the High Court IT wing (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The third machine at a district court location, alongside the two that run CIS, holding a copy of the court's data so that work can continue if the primary fails. E-Filing Rules r.18 is the rule behind it: e-filings are to be stored on an exclusive server maintained under the control and directions of the Court, and a mirror image of them may be kept at a different geographical location for continuity of operations in a disaster, natural calamity or breakdown.
vocabulary.source: The Electronic Filing (E-Filing) Rules, High Court of Punjab and Haryana, rule 18

vocabulary.gloss: The officer who sits with the presiding judge, keeps the daily proceedings and the dates, and raises the objections on a newly filed case before it is registered. Volume III names him separately from the ahlmad: when a holiday or an absence wipes out a day's list, the presiding officer fixes fresh dates in the peshi register himself and hands the register to the reader of the court, who is responsible for telling the parties and witnesses who turn up at a closed court what their new date is. At Panchkula the reader and the ahlmad are two different desks - the reader owns the daily proceedings and the dates, the ahlmad owns registration, process and the record.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.10; described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The CIS function through which the ahlmad turns a judicial order into an actual piece of process. He opens the court and the date, picks the process type from a numbered list (summons to accused, summons to witness, warrant, and a separate entry for the s.138 summons), generates it, and publishes it. Until it is published the document prints 'Draft' across it and cannot be used. Volume III sends the detailed instructions on issuing and serving process to Volume IV, Chapter 8; what the Sanhita requires of the finished article is that it be signed and sealed, or digitally signed if electronic.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-Ci.6 (mode of issuing and serving process); the CIS process-generation module, described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The summons issued to an accused in a s.138 cheque case, which in CIS is a separate template from the ordinary criminal summons and prints in a different, larger format. It has its own service regime: s.144 of the NI Act lets the magistrate direct service by speed post or by a courier approved by a Court of Session, and an acknowledgment or a refusal endorsement lets the court declare service complete. Since the November 2018 amendment to Volume III the magistrate may issue it as an e-summons.
vocabulary.source: NI Act s.144 (mode of service of summons in cheque cases); Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-Ci.2; the distinct CIS template described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The step that turns a generated process from a draft into a live document. Before publishing, the printout carries 'Draft' in large letters and is not acceptable for use; publishing is what commits it. The legal reason is exact: a summons must be in writing signed by the presiding officer and bear the seal of the court, or be in an electronic form bearing the image of the seal or a digital signature, and a warrant must likewise be signed and sealed - a draft carries none of that, so it is not process at all.
vocabulary.source: CIS process-generation workflow, described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026); the requirement it satisfies is in BNSS s.63 and s.72

vocabulary.gloss: What the staff of a Haryana criminal court call the moment the substance of the accusation is put to the accused. In a summons case, and so in a cheque case tried summarily, the particulars of the offence are stated to the accused and he is asked whether he pleads guilty or has any defence, and no formal charge is framed. The everyday phrasing at the desk is that 'charge will be framed' - this and this is alleged against you, you took this much money, what do you say - but in law it is a statement of the particulars, not a charge.
vocabulary.source: BNSS s.274 (substance of accusation to be stated), formerly CrPC s.251; Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-D.2; the local usage recorded firsthand from the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The step a Haryana magistrate's court takes when bailable and non-bailable warrants keep coming back unserved: it writes to the drawer's bank for the KYC address on the account, on the footing that the address the complainant supplied may be false or stale, and then re-issues process to the address the bank returns. No rule prescribes it. It rests on the court's ordinary power to summon a document or thing, and on the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, under which a court may order a party to be at liberty to inspect and take copies of entries in a banker's book.
vocabulary.source: A local coercive-execution step described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026); the powers it rests on are BNSS s.94 and the Bankers' Books Evidence Act s.6

vocabulary.gloss: Sending a finished case file down to the court's record room for keeping. When judgment is pronounced the file comes back to the ahlmad, who binds it, generates the index proforma and consigns it. Volume III's standing requirement is that the record be complete before it is consigned, and that a proceeding which is separate from the main case - a transfer application, and by the same logic a criminal miscellaneous matter - be consigned to the record room separately from it.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 3.18 and rule 26-B.1; the binding-and-sending practice described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The proforma the ahlmad generates out of CIS for a decided case and attaches to the bound file before consigning it to the record room; it lists what the record contains. CIS can produce the same index for a pending file. It is the modern form of Volume III's requirement that the record be complete before it goes to the record room - the retention and indexing rules themselves sit in Rules and Orders Volumes IV and VI-B, which are not yet in this corpus.
vocabulary.source: CIS report, described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026); the completeness requirement it serves is in Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 3.18

vocabulary.gloss: A miscellaneous criminal proceeding taken out of a case that has already been decided and consigned - an application on a NACT file that has gone to the record room, for instance. It is separated from the parent file and becomes a fresh file with its own number, obtained from the filing branch downstairs. Volume III states the same principle for transfer applications: they must form a file separate from the record of the main case and be consigned to the record room separately.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 26-B.1; the CRM separation described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The register of cases instituted in the court. Volume III requires a summary case to be entered in Register No. 1 as soon as it is received in court, and again in the register of summary cases when the accused appears, and makes the ahlmad the keeper of the court's registers subject to a monthly inspection by the presiding officer. In Panchkula the register is now fed from the database: the ahlmad runs the month's institution report out of e-Courts for the establishment and case type, prints it, and pastes it into the physical register.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 2.6 and rule 11-A.14; the e-Courts print-and-paste method described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The case-management reporting the High Court requires of each court, which at Panchkula means a running list of two hundred cases kept updated almost daily out of a pendency of about a thousand, alongside some twenty to thirty other statements. Its rule-level ancestors are in Volume III: every judicial officer must send the High Court a monthly statement of criminal cases pending over one year in the prescribed proforma before the 10th of the following month, with history sheets for the six oldest, and daily progress reports besides. The ahlmad assembles it himself in a spreadsheet, because the reports CIS gives are not aligned with what the High Court asks for.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.12, rule 1-A.13 and rule 1-A.11; the current High Court format described firsthand by the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The summary statement of a court's work - the balance sheet of institution, disposal and pendency - that the staff prepare from the CIS management report for the monthly return to the High Court. The word is the everyday Punjab and Haryana term for such an abstract. Volume III's periodical statements are what it feeds: the monthly statement of criminal cases pending over one year, and the monthly statement of summary cases received and disposed of.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 1-A.12 and rule 2.6; the word and the CIS balance-sheet source recorded firsthand from the criminal ahlmad, Panchkula (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The court official who prepares the written judgment. At Panchkula he is a stenographer-cadre post working inside the courtroom and chambers, distinct from the stenographer outside who takes the daily orders: the steno outside does daily orders, the judgment writer does judgments. He reads the decided file end to end, lifts the case metadata and the template out of CIS, copies the cause title, the parties, the appearances and the facts off the paper file, records the proceedings and the evidence, takes the judge's dictation of the arguments and conclusion in shorthand, types the transcript, and then uploads and e-signs it. Volume III r.25-G.8 recognises the function - stenographers typing evidence and judgments from dictation, and duplicating the free copies in advance - and BNSS s.288(2) allows a summary-trial record or judgment to be prepared by an officer appointed for the purpose, the magistrate signing it. The title itself, and the split between daily-order and judgment stenographers, are establishment practice and appear in no rule.
vocabulary.source: Rules and Orders of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, Volume III (Instructions to Criminal Courts), rule 25-G.8; the post and the split of duties described firsthand by a judgment writer at the Panchkula district courts (PUCAR interview, June 2026)

vocabulary.gloss: The order recorded for a case on each date of hearing - the running order sheet of the file. It is where the court records who appeared and who represented whom, which is why the judgment writer reads the previous daily orders back to build the appearance block of the judgment, cross-checking them against the power of attorney pinned at the back of the file. The daily orders are the stenographer-outside's work; the judgment is the judgment writer's. Nothing about appearance reaches the case record in a queryable form, so it has to be read off the sheet. Staff at Panchkula were heard to call these the 'zimni' orders, the Punjab and Haryana word for the running order sheet.
vocabulary.source: Court practice, Punjab and Haryana district courts; described firsthand by a judgment writer at the Panchkula district courts (PUCAR interview, June 2026). The word 'zimni' is from the machine transcript of the Hindi audio and is recorded as heard; the uploader's own English subtitles render the same thing as 'daily orders'.

vocabulary.gloss: The physical register in which a convicting court records its convictions and takes the convict's acknowledgment for the free copy of the judgment. The convict signs 'copy received' in the corner, and against it the entry has to carry the case and registration number, the accused's name, the sentence and the compensation or fine. It is kept on paper and is not held in CIS. Volume III does not itself prescribe it - the numbered criminal registers sit in Rules and Orders Volumes IV and VI-B, which are not yet in this corpus, and Volume III's own conviction-reporting duty in Chapter 11 Part G covers a listed set of Penal Code and special-Act offences that does not include the Negotiable Instruments Act. At Panchkula it is no longer handwritten: the details are copied out of the judgment into MS Word, shortened, printed, cut and pasted in, a whole month at a time.
vocabulary.source: Court register kept by the judgment writer, Panchkula district courts, described firsthand (PUCAR interview, June 2026). The register series itself is prescribed in Rules and Orders Volumes IV and VI-B, which are not in this corpus; Volume III rule 2.3 and rule 26-B.2 show how it refers registers out.

vocabulary.gloss: The copy of the judgment a convicted accused gets without paying for it, so that he can appeal. Volume III r.1-H.1(vi) requires that whenever an accused is sentenced to imprisonment a copy of the finding and sentence be given to him free of cost soon after the delivery of the judgment, and BNSS s.404(1) says the same of the judgment itself, immediately after pronouncement; s.404(2) makes a certified copy free of cost in every case where the judgment is appealable by the accused, on his application. It matters because BNSS s.423 requires a petition of appeal to be accompanied by a copy of the judgment appealed against. At Panchkula it is treated as a right that needs no request and is handed over the same day, the convict signing for it in the conviction register - which is wider than the letter of s.404(2), and is the shape Volume III r.25-G.2 to r.25-G.4 give the free supply for appeal and revision.
